sources.news_title: Andy Burnham becomes Prime Minister, promising the biggest changes for 40 years
sources.text:
The transfer of power is complete, now he’s got to get on with it before the electorate loses patience. First, it’s about naming the team. Many of Keir Starmer’s highest profile ministers have gone – including Rachel Reeves and David Lammy. The new chancellor, defying most speculation, is John Healey – the former Defence Secretary who resigned last month. The Foreign Secretary is Ed Miliband, Shabana Mahmood remains Home Secretary, and Louise Haigh is Minister for the Cabinet Office.
So, for those who said Andy Burnham might be continuity-Starmer, the new Prime Minister was bold. He intends to be a radical break, promising the biggest political change for 40 years. He will start on Tuesday, with help on the cost of living. Newly-appointed on Monday, he has already talked about tax reductions and social care free at the point of delivery.
So, is the plan coming together? Is it deliverable? And will the bond markets wear it?

Andy Burnham becomes UK’s next prime minister after meeting with King Charles III - Regional Media News
sources.text:
(LONDON) — Andy Burnham officially became British prime minister on Monday — the country’s seventh leader in 10 years — having already been elected as the leader of the country’s Labour Party last week.
Burnham, who until recently was serving as the mayor of Greater Manchester, succeeded outgoing Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Speaking outside the prime minister’s official residence — 10 Downing Street — on Monday morning, Starmer said, “Today I am here to offer my resignation and close the book on my time as prime minister. My work is done.”
“I thank the British people for the opportunity to serve. I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything that we have achieved. Thank you very much,” Starmer added.
Of his successor, the outgoing prime minister said, “I now pass the baton to Andy Burnham, I wish him every success. He has my full support.”
After his address, Starmer traveled the short distance to Buckingham Palace to formally inform King Charles III of his resignation. Burnham then also traveled to palace where the king asked him to form a government.
The new prime minister then traveled to Downing Street to give his first address, telling the assembled press that Britain must show “that we can regain our stability.”
Burnham said his appointment will serve as “a circuit-breaker” for the country, pledging to deliver a new political and economic model and a 10-year plan.
Among the new prime’s commitments were to address cost of living concerns, help young people into work, end homelessness, re-industrialize the country, put “life’s essentials back under public control” and push for more local powers.
Through the rest of Monday, Burnham is expected to begin appointing cabinet ministers from Number 10.
Starmer announced that he would step down in June, following months of domestic political turmoil. Despite leading Labour to a historic majority in parliament in the 2024 general election, Starmer faced persistent external and internal criticism over his perceived failure to deliver rapid change after 14 years of Conservative Party rule in Britain.
Many in Starmer’s party had written to the prime minister asking him to step down following local elections in May, which saw the party lose more than 1,000 seats on local councils, results that were widely interpreted as a repudiation by British voters of Labour’s performance under the prime minister’s leadership.
Starmer long said he intended to see out his full five-year. Announcing his resignation in June, Starmer said, “The question my party is asking now is whether I am best placed to lead us into the next general election. I have heard the answer of my parliamentary party to that question, and I accept that answer with good grace.”
Burnham was the only candidate in the subsequent leadership election, ultimately winning nominations from 379 of the 403 Labour members of parliament — of the 650 MPs in total — in the House of Commons.
In accepting the leadership of Labour last week, Burnham said his mission was “to bring back hope” and address decades of economic inequality plus falling living standards.
“We must recognize that this generation of politicians — myself included — have failed to challenge a political culture and an economic model that simply doesn’t work well enough for ordinary people,” he said.
Burnham will become the seventh leader to take the reins of the country in 10 years, a reflection of the political and economic turbulence that has beset the country since the Brexit vote in 2016.
The incoming prime minister said he would also make British politics “less toxic, adding, “I will work to build a new politics. The country is crying out for it.”
Burnham, 56, was born in the Lancashire region of northern England. Burnham started out as a journalist, writing for trade magazines, before transitioning to work as a Labour parliamentary researcher while in his early 20s.
Burnham rose through the party ranks before being elected as the MP for his hometown of Leigh, in Greater Manchester, in 2001. He held that seat for 16 years, during which time he was appointed to several cabinet positions under Prime Ministers Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.
During Labour’s years in opposition, Burnham bid to become Labour leader twice, but was defeated by — and then served in shadow cabinets of — Labour leaders Ed Miliband and Jeremy Corbyn.
In 2017, Burnham left parliament to become the mayor of Greater Manchester. In his victory speech, Burnham heralded what he called “the dawn of a new era, not just for this city region but for politics in our country. It has been too London-centric for too long. The old political and party structures haven’t delivered for all people and for all places.”
Burnham is associated with the center left of the Labour Party, and has described himself as a socialist. Burnham’s time as Manchester mayor saw him emerge as a major proponent of shifting investment and political power out of London, and earned him the nickname “the King of the North.”
ABC News’ Kevin Shalvey contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham takes office as British prime minister, promising stability | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Andy Burnham takes office as British prime minister, promising stability
LONDON >> Andy Burnham became Britain’s seventh prime minister in a decade today, pledging to reshape its politics to deliver a new economic model and revive a nation “fed up” with a revolving door of leaders.
In front of dozens of supporters outside his new office and residence at 10 Downing Street, Burnham said politicians had failed to bring the stability needed to raise living standards, something he said he would change, with both immediate measures and a longer-term plan to be drawn up later this year.
Speaking without notes, Burnham delivered a domestic-focused speech aimed at offering hope to a nation that has, like many European countries, struggled for years with soaring prices and anaemic economic growth.
He did not touch on foreign affairs.
“I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you, and I want to be honest with you, we have not been good enough and we need to be better,” he said, dispensing with the lectern that prime ministers generally use.
Burnham pledged to use his premiership as a “circuit-breaker for Britain,” arguing that a new model was needed to rebuild the country, which has been in political turmoil since voting in 2016 to leave the European Union.

Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Just over an hour after his predecessor and Labour colleague Keir Starmer had made his farewell speech to say “My work is done,” the 56-year-old former Greater Manchester mayor entered Downing Street, where he said his team would tackle his first priority: to end rough sleeping.
The major challenges will then lie ahead.
Burnham must first unveil his cabinet — already the subject of much debate in the Labour Party — and then tackle a long list of problems ranging from high levels of illegal immigration to underperforming utility firms.
Starmer, ousted by his own lawmakers a month ago, said his work as prime minister was “the privilege of my life” and that he wished Burnham every success, with “my full support.”
Burnham did not refer to Starmer in his speech, instead focusing on how he will bring change.
But he acknowledged that some of his program would take time.
In his short address, thin on policy detail, Burnham said he would release a long-term plan for the next decade within months and repeated his pledge to build more public housing and to help bring down welfare spending to fund higher defence investment.
Opposition parties suggested he would need to win a national election to get a mandate to implement it.
But he promised to unveil more immediate measures on Tuesday to ease everyday pressures on Britons, and explain how he will pay for them.
Speaking to reporters later today, Burnham said he was finalizing the details of those measures, which he described as “things that people will feel and feel quite quickly.”
“It won’t solve everything, it won’t take all of the pressure off, but it just shows the direction of travel and … about helping them out,” he said, not long after arriving in Downing Street and before he started unveiling his top team.
Dubbed ‘King of the North’ for his dogged defence of the Manchester region’s interests, Burnham received messages of congratulations from foreign leaders, including European leaders who called for closer ties.
His first phone call was with President Donald Trump, a White House official said.
Burnham also said he wanted to speak to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for whose country he expressed continued support.
Labour lawmakers see Burnham as one of the few figures capable of tackling the threat from veteran Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK – something they doubted the unpopular Starmer could do.
A key first decision will be Burnham’s choice of finance minister after Rachel Reeves was one of several Starmer allies to say she was leaving the government.
Friction in this axis of government has brought down previous administrations.
An early frontrunner for the position, energy security and net zero minister Ed Miliband, has been the object of hostile briefing, and interior minister Shabana Mahmood now appears favourite for the job.
On Sunday, Burnham scrapped plans for all employees to be required to hold a digital identity document, a scheme designed to tackle illegal migration but deemed a “fiasco” by a cross-party committee of lawmakers.
More attention will be paid to decisions on taxation and spending, oil and gas and underperforming utility companies, where Burnham wants stronger public control.
Additional reporting by Sam Tabahriti.

sources.news_title: New PM Burnham vows 10-year plan for Britain
sources.text:
New British Prime Minister Andy Burnham yesterday promised to set out a 10-year-plan for Britain, to ease the cost of living crisis and outlined policy goals, including an end to sleeping on the streets.
Accompanied by his wife, Marie-France van Heel, Burnham earlier met King Charles III at Buckingham Palace to become the head of government after Keir Starmer resigned.
Burnham, 56, arrived at Downing Street to resounding applause from supporters and acknowledged he was the country’s seventh prime minister since the start of 2016.
Photo: Reuters
Britain needed to show the world it could “regain stability,” he said, vowing to offer “a new political model” and “build a new economy.”
In foreign policy goals, he told broadcasters earlier his first calls would be to US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, to whom he would offer reassurance that “I will be with him 100 percent.”
In his brief speech outside Downing Street, the new Labour leader said he would “bring forward a new plan for Britain, a 10-year plan,” without giving specifics.
Naming short-term goals, he promised to “give people some breathing space now, some help with the cost of living.”
He also said his first instruction would be a pledge to “end rough sleeping,” a measure he attempted to implement as a regional mayor in northern England, although it was not fully successful.
Other announcements included a pledge to reindustrialize Britain through public procurement and to build more public housing.
Starmer departed Downing Street earlier, insisting his short time in office had made Britain a better place.
“I am confident that Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago,” Starmer told reporters in his farewell speech outside Downing Street.
“I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything that we have achieved,” he added.
Burnham faces an in-tray overflowing with challenges with little time to make his mark with a nationwide election due in 2029.
In an interview with the Times published late on Sunday, Burnham said he wanted to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil.
“What we’ve been doing hasn’t been working. That’s the way I see it,” he said.
“I am going to try and do things in a different way,” he said.
The focus now turns to his senior Cabinet appointments, with all eyes on who is to replace Rachel Reeves as chancellor of the exchequer.
The former mayor of Greater Manchester, nicknamed the “King of the North,” has been parachuted in by the Labour Party, after Starmer resigned last month, with lawmakers viewing him as the party’s best chance of reining in Nigel Farage’s anti-immigration Reform UK party.
Among Burnham’s most urgent challenges will be a tepid economy, high government borrowing costs, a ballooning welfare bill and irregular migrants arriving in small boats that have fueled support for Reform.
Unpredictable energy prices due to the US-Iran war and volatile relations with the United States undeer Trump also threaten to buffet his premiership.
Burnham told the Times he would take a “different approach to public spending, and to running the economy — more focused on early investment, early intervention, setting people up for success, and much less paying for failure.”

sources.news_title: Burnham talks a good game, now he must deliver - and quickly
sources.text:
Andy Burnham talks a good game, now he must deliver - and quickly
The new Prime Minister is blessed with strong communication skills - but he must back that up with radical action and he doesn't have long, writes Liam Thorp
There were two speeches today - and they were very different.
This morning, Sir Keir Starmer spoke from outside Downing Street as Prime Minister for the last time. He thanked his family, friends and colleagues for supporting him during his tumultuous two-years in charge and even had some warm wishes for the man who is about to replace him.
Like many of Starmer's speeches, there was nothing inherently wrong with Starmer's speech, but no one can argue that he is a natural communicator or a soaring orator. Those of us who have met Sir Keir in the flesh will know he is far more effective at delivering his message in person than he is in public.
What we saw around an hour later from Andy Burnham showed one element of why Labour MPs have thrown their support behind him with such vigour and why they believe he is the one who can change their fortunes.
Politics must be about a heck of a lot more than just communication, but being able to connect with people in an authentic way has always been important and feels increasingly vital in an era of rolling news and social media obsessions.
Burnham showed in his remarks as he arrived in Downing Street that he is already comfortably ahead of his predecessor in terms of the skill set he brings in this department.
Speaking without notes and without the formality of the lectern, he cut a more comfortable figure than the man he is replacing. He spoke with passion and clarity in words that people can understand. This is his great skill as a politician, setting out a clear vision for the future in a language that people can digest, even if they don't take notice of the day-to-day minutia of policy.
But in many ways today's speech was the easy part for the new man in Number 10.
He has made these arguments before, he has set out his vision already - yes he will have been nervous about the gravity of the situation and the history that weighed on his shoulders, but nailing the speech is just the start.
Because he's right, people are fed up of politics. They are fed up of a Prime Ministerial merry-go-round that is a symptom of a failing democratic model that has lost the ability to improve people's lives.
He will never be as popular or as powerful as the moment he delivered that speech - by the end of today as his cabinet choices become clear, he will have lost support in some spaces and this will continue as he continues to make the sort of trade-offs that are inevitable in the position he now holds.
This is why he must deliver on his promise to be radical and to deliver changes and he must do it immediately.
Promising to end rough sleeping across the country is an enormously ambitious pledge - and those in Greater Manchester who saw him say something very similar when he became mayor there may have their doubts - but like with his other plans, the action must match the rhetoric.
Andy Burnham is a very different politician and person to the Blair/Brown-era cabinet minister who was often accused of 'flip flopping' and changing his positions - nearly a decade as a regional mayor has certainly cemented his central political philosophy.
But as many have said before, articulating that philosophy and delivering the changes required are very different things, especially when you will be hit with a million different priorities from global conflicts to party-infighting from day one.
That's why he must remain clear-eyed and focussed on his big idea at all times. He says he wants to rewire the country and fundamentally change the way politics works, so that it better supports people in the places like those that made him who he is.
It all sounds good and for those of us who have been calling for a redistribution of power for a long time, it is very encouraging to hear. But breaking up the Whitehall machine won't come easily and there will be plenty who try to stand in his way.
For the good of the country and all those who believe this place can be better - he simply must deliver - and quickly.

sources.news_title: Rents Could Be Frozen Under Moves To Help Struggling Brits, Hints Andy Burnham
sources.text:
Rents could be frozen as part of attempts to help Brits struggling with the cost of living, Andy Burnham has indicated.
The new prime minister is also looking at ways to bring down energy bills and cap bus fares to show his government is on the side of ordinary people.
He has also set out his ambition of ending rough sleeping in the UK during his time in office.
Burnham is expected to unveil a package of measures tomorrow aimed at putting more money in people’s pockets as he aims to hit the ground running after replacing Keir Starmer in No.10.
In his first speech in Downing Street, Burnham said he wanted to “give people some breathing space”.
Speaking to journalists in the No.10 garden afterwards, Burnham was asked if that would include measures on bus fares, energy bills and rent freezes.
He said: “We are looking at all of those things, but we will make more announcements tomorrow. We’re just finalising the details.
“It’s premature to say it will be any one of those particular things. We just want to do some things that people will feel and feel quite quickly. It won’t solve everything, it won’t take all of the pressure off but it just shows the direction of travel and that we’re serious about helping them out.”
Bringing in rent controls is one of the Green Party’s key policies, but critics say it could lead to a shortage of properties as landlords respond by taking them off the market.
Ben Beadle, chief executive of the National Residential Landlords Association, said: “Rent controls would choke off supply in the private rented sector, making it harder to meet the prime minister’s welcome ambition to end rough sleeping.
“The reality is that rent increases have fallen by two thirds over the past two years at exactly the time when supply is better meeting tenant demand. Rent controls would undermine all of this.”
Meanwhile, Burnham also failed to rule out increasing the top rate of income tax to 50p in the pound.
However, that would be a clear breach of Labour’s election manifesto, which he has insisted he will stick to.
The new PM also said he wanted to “fix” the social care system before he leaves office.
He said the NHS was spending billions of pounds a year looking after elderly people stuck in hospitals because there is nowhere else for them to go.
“I am ready to use some of my political capital on this issue,” he said. “I’ll be blunt with you. I would not want to leave office having done what Westminster has done, not just not just for 15 years actually, I think you’re getting close to 30 years.
“It’s not defensible. How many people have lost their homes and their savings in that time? We need to face it and fix it.”

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham pledges end to political instability as he becomes UK PM
sources.text:
Andy Burnham pledges end to political instability as he becomes UK PM
Britain’s seventh PM in a decade pledged major changes in bid to see off populist forces that are making large gains.
Andy Burnham has set out his vision for Britain as he took over as prime minister.
Burnham’s appointment was confirmed on Monday as he met King Charles III at Buckingham Palace. Becoming the United Kingdom’s seventh premier in a decade, he pledged to end the political instability that has plagued the country and promised to instigate major change.

- list 3 of 4Andy Burnham’s in-tray: The challenges facing the new UK PM
- list 4 of 4What’s next as Andy Burnham takes over as UK’s next prime minister?
Burnham replaces Keir Starmer, who was ousted just two years after winning a landslide election victory amid ongoing gains by populist forces.
“Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again,” Burnham said after arriving at his official home, 10 Downing Street in London, to rapturous applause. “We have not been good enough and we need to be better.”
The former mayor of Greater Manchester said he was “fed up” with the country’s revolving door of leadership, which should invite “a moment for reflection and new resolution” for British politics.
Starmer was ousted by his peers about a month ago. On leaving office, he labelled his work as prime minister “the privilege of my life” and said that Burnham has his “full support”.
Burnham did not refer to Starmer in his speech, instead focusing on how he will implement change.
“We will make this moment a circuit-breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years. A new political model and a new economic model,” Burnham declared.
Promising Britons “some breathing space now”, he promised to announce measures this week to help tackle the cost of living.
The first instruction he will issue is “to end rough sleeping in our country”.
A 10-year plan would come later in 2026, he added. He was careful, however, to note that his promised measures to help with the cost of living would not mean “taking risks with the economy”.
Regarding foreign policy, Burnham said Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will be one of the first foreign leaders he will speak with to assure him that British support will remain “resolute” under his premiership.
“I will be with him [Zelenskyy] 100 percent, as Keir Starmer has been, and Keir has done quite an incredible job in not just backing Ukraine, but being there in a personal way,” Burnham said. “And I will be absolutely there for him in the same way.”
The new PM also indicated he would have an early call with United States President Donald Trump. A White House official said shortly afterwards that the two leaders had spoken.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang was quick to offer congratulations to Burnham and spoke of hope for cooperation, the state-run Xinhua news agency said.
Changing cabinet line up
Burnham has begun announcing his senior cabinet appointments, while several figures from Starmer’s government were quick to depart.
Former Defence Secretary John Healey has been named finance minister after Rachel Reeves was fired.
Healey resigned from Starmer’s government last month after accusing him of failing to invest enough in defence. His appointment suggests the new government will raise spending.
The Deputy Prime Minister and Justice Secretary David Lammy also left government, with Business Secretary Peter Kyle also sacked, according to Sky News.
The “King of the North”, as Burnham has been nicknamed due to his time leading Manchester and supporting working-class issues, has been backed by the Labour Party as the party’s best chance of reining in Nigel Farage’s populist, anti-immigration party Reform UK.
Just two years after centre-left Labour won a landslide in elections, Reform UK leads in the polls, with the next national vote due in 2029.

sources.news_title: 'Time for hope' says West of England mayor as Burnham becomes PM
sources.text:
'Moment not just about Andy' says mayor as Burnham becomes UK's sixth Prime Minister in decade
Helen Godwin welcomed her party's new leader but said the region wants to 'feel change'
The West of England mayor has said it is "a time for hope" as Andy Burnham became Britain's sixth Prime Minister in a decade on Monday. Labour's Helen Godwin welcomed her party's new leader, but also warned the moment was "not just about Andy" and that people in the West Country "want and need to see and feel change".
"It's about the direction of our country, including the West of England as the fastest-growing regional economy over the last five years," she said.
"Over the years, I have worked closely with Andy Burnham. He already knows our region well, which will set him in good stead as Prime Minister."
The mayor's comments came as the former Manchester mayor made his first speech since taking over as Labour leader from Sir Keir Starmer.
Speaking outside No 10 Downing Street on Monday - without notes or the customary lectern - Burnham pledged to "build a new economy".
He promised a 10-year plan for the UK and vowed to unveil a suite of cost-of-living support measures to help British people, potentially as early as Tuesday.
The new Labour leader also said his government would put "life's essentials back under stronger public control" and breathe new life into the nation's industrial heartlands.
"We will make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years, a new political model and a new economic model," he said.
"We will take power out of here and carry it into every postcode in the land, so that they can do more, and in doing more, build a new economy where we put life's essentials back under stronger public control."
Ms Godwin, who heads up the West of England Combined Authority - covering Bristol, Bath and North East Somerset and South Gloucestershire - said on Monday she would "look forward" to working with the new Prime Minister to "make a difference for local residents".
"We have a proper plan to secure further investment and create more jobs here, working with ministers and officials across the new government to get greater funding just as we have done over the last 15 months," she added.
"Whether it's taking more control of our buses, delivering mass transit, or more devolution from Westminster."
Sir Keir formally submitted his resignation earlier on Monday, announcing "his work was done" and it had been a "privilege" to serve in Downing Street.

sources.news_title: Britain’s New Labour PM Promises More State Control
sources.text:
Andy Burnham became Britain’s new prime minister on Monday, promising to return power to ordinary people while setting out plans for a larger state, greater public ownership and closer control of the economy.
Burnham formally took office after King Charles III invited him to form a government. He replaces Keir Starmer after winning the leadership of the governing Labour Party, meaning British voters will not have a direct say on their new prime minister until the next general election.
He is Britain’s seventh prime minister since the country voted to leave the European Union in 2016—a period of political instability that has seen six changes of leader in ten years.
Speaking outside 10 Downing Street, Burnham acknowledged that voters were “fed up with politics” and admitted that Labour had “not been good enough”.
“We will make this moment a circuit-breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years,” he said, promising both “a new political model and a new economic model”.
The new prime minister blamed many of Britain’s problems on decisions made during the 1980s, when Margaret Thatcher’s Conservative government privatised state industries and reduced the power of trade unions. Burnham said political power had become too concentrated in London, while deindustrialisation had left large parts of the country in decline.
He promised to transfer greater authority from the central government to local areas and place essential services under “stronger public control”. A ten-year “Plan for Britain”, including measures to support domestic industry through government purchasing, will be published later this year.
Burnham also announced that his first instruction as prime minister would be to end rough sleeping. Further measures intended to ease the cost-of-living crisis will be unveiled on Tuesday, alongside an explanation of how they will be funded.
Notably absent from his first speech was any mention of immigration or border control, despite opinion polls identifying immigration as one of the issues of greatest concern to British voters. Burnham offered no indication of whether he would reduce legal migration, stop illegal Channel crossings or make it easier to deport foreign criminals.
As political commentator Matt Goodwin has pointed out, the central promise of Burnham’s premiership already contains a considerable contradiction. Although he says he will return power to the British people, his government remains committed to institutions and policies that place important decisions beyond their direct control.
Labour has shown no willingness to withdraw Britain from the European Convention on Human Rights, whose rules have repeatedly been used to prevent the deportation of illegal migrants and foreign criminals. Burnham also takes office as his party seeks closer alignment with the European Union, despite the 17.4 million people who voted for Brexit in 2016.
His proposed expansion of public ownership and state intervention would meanwhile hand more power to government bodies, regulators and officials. Simply transferring authority from London to regional administrations does not necessarily give ordinary citizens any greater control, as the records of the devolved governments in Scotland and Wales demonstrate.
Burnham must also reconcile his expensive domestic programme with growing demands for higher defence spending. Warren Stephens, the US ambassador to Britain, warned the new government against delaying investment in AUKUS, the nuclear submarine partnership between Britain, the United States and Australia.
President Donald Trump has separately urged Britain to develop its North Sea oil and gas reserves, arguing that cheaper domestic energy could help address the country’s economic difficulties. Labour has instead pursued net-zero policies that restrict new drilling.
Burnham has promised to maintain Britain’s commitment to NATO, its nuclear deterrent and its alliance with the United States. He has also suggested that defence spending should be used to support British manufacturers.
The new prime minister therefore enters Downing Street promising national renewal and popular control, but leading a Labour government committed to higher spending, an expanding state, continued rule by foreign courts and closer ties with Brussels.
Whether Burnham returns power to British voters—or merely redistributes it among another collection of officials and public bodies—may define his premiership.

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham becomes UK’s seventh prime minister in a decade after Starmer resigns
sources.text:
Andy Burnham becomes UK’s seventh prime minister in a decade after Starmer resigns
Loading article...
LONDON (AP) — Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged his precarious perch Monday as the seventh British leader in just over a decade as he set out an ambitious but vague vision to create a new political and economic establishment.
Burnham used his inaugural speech as prime minister to renew his theme of decentralising power, as he promised to end street sleeping by homeless people.
He said he would deliver a “circuit breaker” for a system he says has taken wrong turns since the 1980s, when many public services were privatised.
“We will change politics to make it more collaborative, more about problem-solving than point-scoring,” he said.
“We will take power out of here and carry it into every postcode in the land so that they can do more and in doing more, build a new economy where we put life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again.”
After weeks as leader-in-waiting, Burnham officially became prime minister during a meeting with King Charles III at Buckingham Palace, where the monarch asked him to form a government.
He succeeded Keir Starmer, who stepped down just two years after winning a landslide election victory, on a day when Britain’s political turbulence gave way, at least temporarily, to smooth choreography.
Buckingham Palace has released a photo of the king and Burnham shaking hands.
The ceremony known as “kissing hands” marks the transfer of power, but it didn’t actually involve any hand kissing.
Burnham said he was “acutely conscious” of the revolving door he was walking through at 10 Downing Street.
“This is a moment for reflection and new resolution,” he said. “It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge. Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again, and that is our challenge to make politics work, to make it work better.”
Burnham became the seventh UK prime minister since 2016 in a now well-rehearsed handover after replacing Starmer as leader of the center-left governing Labour Party on Friday.
Starmer announced last month he would resign after missteps and judgment errors that eroded his standing with his party and the public.
Just over an hour earlier, Starmer made a short farewell speech in the same place outside the prime minister’s residence, saying “my work is done.”

sources.news_title: ‘King Of The North’ Andy Burnham Becomes Britain’s New Prime Minister
sources.text:
Andy Burnham officially became the United Kingdom’s new prime minister on Monday, taking office after Keir Starmer stepped down as Labour Party leader following mounting political setbacks.
Burnham, 56, was formally invited by King Charles III to form a government during a ceremony at Buckingham Palace, becoming the 116th British prime minister and the seventh person to hold the office in just over a decade.
The leadership transition did not require a general election because Britain’s parliamentary system allows the governing party to replace its leader — and therefore the prime minister — during an existing parliamentary term.
Burnham Promises ‘Circuit Breaker’ for Britain
Speaking outside 10 Downing Street after being sworn in, Burnham pledged sweeping political and economic reforms, describing his administration as a “circuit breaker for Britain.”
“We will make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years,” Burnham said, per Fox News. “A new political model and a new economic model.”
Burnham acknowledged growing public frustration with politics after years of leadership changes.
“I know people at home are fed up with politics,” he said, per Fox. “I hear you, and I want to be honest with you — we have not been good enough, and we need to be better. We will be.”
Unlike recent prime ministers, Burnham delivered his inaugural address without using the traditional lectern outside No. 10, opting instead for a more informal presentation.
Focus on Cost Of Living and Devolution
Burnham said his government would prioritize reducing living costs, tackling homelessness, and shifting more decision-making authority away from Westminster and into local communities.
He said his first instruction as prime minister would be to end “rough sleeping” across the country.
Later this year, Burnham plans to unveil a 10-year strategy for Britain focused on decentralizing political power and rebuilding the economy.
His agenda includes expanding local control over transportation, housing, and infrastructure while increasing public oversight of essential services — an approach he has previously described as “Manchesterism,” reflecting policies he championed during his tenure as mayor of Greater Manchester.
Starmer Steps Aside
Earlier Monday, outgoing Prime Minister Keir Starmer delivered a farewell address outside Downing Street before traveling to Buckingham Palace to formally resign.
“My work is done,” Starmer said, per Fox.
He thanked supporters and wished Burnham success.
“As I now pass the baton to Andy Burnham, I wish him every success,” Starmer said. “He has my full support.”
Starmer’s departure comes just two years after Labour won a landslide general election victory. His leadership was weakened by a series of election defeats, policy reversals, and political controversies.
A Familiar Face Returns to National Politics
Burnham’s rise to Britain’s highest office caps a lengthy political comeback.
After losing Labour’s leadership contest in 2015, he left frontline national politics and spent nine years serving as mayor of Greater Manchester, where he became one of the country’s most recognizable regional leaders and earned the nickname “King of the North.”
Before becoming mayor, Burnham served in several senior government positions and held multiple Cabinet roles under previous Labour governments.
More recently, he returned to Parliament after winning a special election and was elected Labour leader unopposed following Starmer’s resignation.
Challenges Await New Government
Burnham inherits a government facing significant domestic and international challenges.
Among his immediate priorities are addressing Britain’s ongoing cost-of-living pressures, improving the National Health Service, boosting economic growth, and managing continued debates over immigration and Britain’s relationship with Europe.
His government also faces increasing political pressure from Reform UK, led by Nigel Farage, which has gained support in recent opinion polls.
On foreign policy, Burnham has pledged to maintain Britain’s commitments to NATO, support Ukraine, and preserve the country’s nuclear deterrent while managing relations with President Donald Trump’s administration.
The next general election is not required until 2029, although Burnham has the authority to call one earlier if he chooses.
Provided by Dallas Express

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham officially appointed UK Prime Minister
sources.text:
Andy Burnham was officially appointed Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on Monday after being invited by King Charles III to form a government, succeeding Keir Starmer following the latter's resignation.
Buckingham Palace confirmed that Burnham accepted the King's invitation after an audience at the palace, formally becoming Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury.
Before traveling to Buckingham Palace to tender his resignation, Starmer delivered his final address outside 10 Downing Street, thanking the British public and reflecting on his time in office. He said he was leaving with "good grace" and "a smile," adding that Britain was "stronger and fairer than it was two years ago." Starmer also praised the "resolve, grit, decency and compassion" shown by people across the country during his premiership.
Shortly afterward, Burnham arrived at Downing Street and delivered his first speech as Prime Minister, pledging to restore confidence in politics and improve living standards.
"We need a new national sense of unity," Burnham said, promising to place care for people at the center of government. He also said his administration would act as a "circuit breaker" to reform systems that he argued had failed for decades, while committing to tackling rough sleeping, increasing affordable housing, reforming mental health services and education, and unveiling further measures to address the cost of living.
Burnham acknowledged the frequency of changes in British leadership over the past decade, saying politicians "need to be better" and pledging to restore greater stability and public trust.
Burnham assumes office after winning the Labour Party leadership unopposed following growing pressure on Starmer to step aside. His appointment makes him the seventh British prime minister in the past decade. Cabinet appointments are expected later Monday.
Burnham's rise to power is expected to signal the further deterioration of UK-Israel ties. The new leader has previously indicated that his government would take a firmer approach toward Israel than his predecessor.
Earlier this month, Burnham apologized for what he described as Labour's initial response to Israel's military campaign in Gaza, saying, "My party didn't get it right, and I am sorry about that." He also pledged to consider additional sanctions against individuals and entities and to examine restrictions on trade involving goods from what he described as Israeli settlements.
At the same time, Burnham reiterated his condemnation of the October 7 Hamas massacre and said there was "no contradiction between a zero-tolerance approach to antisemitism and holding the Netanyahu government to account." He declined to characterize the war in Gaza as genocide, saying such a determination should be made by international courts rather than politicians.

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham becomes UK Prime Minister
sources.text:
Andy Burnham becomes UK Prime Minister: Impact on Brits abroad
By Adam Woodward • Published: 20 Jul 2026 • 15:43 • 3 minutes read
Andy Burnham becomes UK Prime Minister. Credit: Lauren Hurley - Nº10
When your Spanish neighbours ask ¿Quién es Andy Burnham?, have you worked out what you are going to say yet?
Andy Burnham walked through the big black door of 10 Downing Street this morning as Britain’s seventh prime minister in a decade. King Charles invited him to form a government after he took the Labour leadership unchallenged. No general election decided the change for the 6th time in a decade. British residents living in Spain now watch closely for any shift in policy that could touch their daily lives, yet clear signals stay strangely absent.
Rapid rise without public vote
Burnham left the Greater Manchester mayoralty, won a by-election on June 19, re-entered Parliament within days and became party leader last Friday once his only rival stepped aside. Five of the last six prime ministerial switches happened without ordinary voters casting ballots on the choice. Cameron, May, Johnson, Truss, Sunak, Starmer and now Burnham give an average stay of roughly seventeen months. Larry the cat has already outlasted six occupants and met his seventh today. Burnham arrived promising to end the churn. Every predecessor offered similar words on the same front doorstep.
No direct statements on Spain or Gibraltar
Searches of public records show Burnham has offered almost nothing specific about Spain or Gibraltar. Old social media posts from more than a decade ago touched Spanish football in passing. Sovereignty questions and post-Brexit residency matters for British nationals in Spain simply do not appear in his record. Foreign policy comments overall remain thin compared with domestic themes of devolution, northern England and public services. Mention Andy Burnham to Brits living in Spain, and almost certainly you will get an eye-roll as reply. Not only did no one get to vote him in, there wasn’t even a manifesto published to indicate his priorities. So, for UK expats, shrugging shoulders on the subject has become standard.
Pro-European leanings but domestic priority first
Burnham holds a long-term interest in closer European ties and has even spoken of rejoining the European Union at some future point. Recent campaign remarks, however, played down any quick return and stressed domestic focus instead. Continuity looks likely on Ukraine and NATO. British residents in Spain who rely on settled status, healthcare access, pension payments and easier travel therefore face no announced reforms, and few seem to have much of an opinion of Burnham either way. Any movement would almost certainly arrive through wider UK-EU talks rather than dedicated measures for the expatriate community.
Money rails outlast leaders
One detail from Burnham’s past stands apart: a recorded pledge to turn Manchester into a Web3 powerhouse. National digital-asset rules already sit with the Financial Conduct Authority, and Labour froze crypto donations earlier this year. Independent work on a digital sovereign bond and Bank of England stablecoin rules continues on decade-long timelines. Those projects will outlive the average recent occupant of Number 10, of course. For Britons abroad the political noise in London changes little; the practical systems that govern cross-border life move much more slowly.
Burnham begins, acutely aware of the turnover that brought him here. Aides say he wants to break the cycle. But, British residents in Spain have heard similar vows before. Without fresh statements directed at their interests, daily realities of residency, services and travel look set to continue under existing frameworks while the new government settles in.
Another day, another PM. If the neighbours ask about Andy Burnham? A Northern English bloke who ran Manchester like a slightly left-wing mayor, then magically became Labour leader and PM this week without bothering the voters. Britain’s on its seventh leader in ten years – a quicker turnover than your tapas bars on a Friday night. Pro-EU in theory, but mostly obsessed with fixing potholes up north. Expect more stability promises and zero mention of Spanish relations.

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham begins as UK PM with stability and unity pledge
sources.text:
Andy Burnham begins as UK PM with stability and unity pledge
Andy Burnham began his term as Prime Minister by pledging stability, unity and wider devolution. His first speech signalled an effort to rebuild trust in politics and ease pressure on households.
Andy Burnham began his tenure as the UK’s new Prime Minister on Monday by acknowledging the political instability that has taken Britain through a string of leaders in recent years. Soon after a customary meeting with King Charles III, Burnham used his first address outside 10 Downing Street to call for stability, better politics and a renewed sense of national unity.
In a speech that also set out his early priorities, Burnham said power would be shifted away from Westminster and towards regions across the country, while the cost-of-living crisis would be tackled by making essentials more affordable. He also departed from convention by speaking extempore and without the traditional lectern used for prime ministerial speeches at Downing Street.
"I am acutely conscious that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street, the seventh Prime Minister since 2016, making this a moment for reflection and new resolution," Burnham said in his inaugural address. "It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge. Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again, and that is our challenge, to make politics work, to make it work better... Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose, and positivity," he said.
He also addressed public frustration with politics directly. "I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you, and I want to be honest with you, we have not been good enough, and we need to be better. We will be," he said.
Among the central themes of the speech were regional devolution and the rising pressure on household finances. "We will take power out of here and carry it into every postcode in the land so that they can do more. And in doing more, build a new economy, where we put life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again," Burnham said.
This marks the third attempt at the top job for the 56-year-old politician, who had earlier failed in Labour leadership contests in 2010 and 2015. He returned to Westminster politics last month after winning a by-election at Makerfield in northern England, a contest presented as a test of his ability to push back against the growing threat from the far-right Reform UK. In his maiden speech as Prime Minister, he also promised a new "10-year plan", signalling his intention to lead into the next general election expected by 2029.
Burnham was born in Merseyside in north-west England to a telephone engineer father and a GP surgery receptionist mother, and grew up in Cheshire. A University of Cambridge graduate, he entered politics as a researcher and special adviser to a Labour veteran before winning his first general election as MP for Leigh in Greater Manchester in 2001. He rose through government under Gordon Brown, serving as Chief Secretary to the Treasury, Culture Secretary and Health Secretary. After Labour lost power in 2010, he served in Ed Miliband’s shadow cabinet, then lost the 2015 leadership race to Jeremy Corbyn before resigning as an MP in 2017 to pursue his mayoral bid in Greater Manchester.
As mayor, Burnham became widely known as the "King of the North", a reference to the American fantasy drama 'Game of Thrones'. He won the Labour leadership unopposed last week. During his time in Greater Manchester, he led a major delegation to India in 2019 and underlined the importance of closer ties, saying: "India is a key market in Greater Manchester’s internationalisation strategy as it presents significant opportunities to the city-region, but these opportunities are mutual, and Greater Manchester is also helping India with its own economic growth plans."
Burnham’s family is expected to split time between London and northern England. His Dutch-born wife, Marie-France van Heel, and their three children in their 20s — Jimmy, Rosie and Anne-Marie — are linked to his proposal for a "No. 10 North", which is aimed at ensuring that power is not concentrated only at 10 Downing Street. His opening day in office brought together that broader message: a promise of stability, a push to spread power beyond Westminster and a call to rebuild trust in politics.
With PTI Inputs

sources.news_title: Dale Vince is 'overwhelmingly positive and excited' as Andy Burnham becomes PM
sources.text:
Dale Vince said he was 'overwhelmingly positive and excited' as Andy Burnham beame Prime Minister on Monday.
Mr Burnham promised to win over voters 'fed up with politics' and show the world that the UK can once again be a source of stability.
He used his first speech as Prime Minister in Downing Street to promise to take power out of Westminster and give the public greater control over “life’s essentials”.
Vince, wearing a shirt saying “chips are vegan” told the Press Association in Downing Street: “I’m feeling excited. I think Andy Burnham is going to do great things.
“There’s so many things that can be done. The new economic model he’s talking about is something that we’ve been working on recently. We’ve got a working title, “peoplenomics”, and it’s about putting people first in the economy, making sure that they can afford their energy bills and water works and they have a house so that they can contribute to the economy.”
Specifying which policies he would suggest, the multi-millionaire said: “Energy market reform which will half our energy bills, saving billions of pounds (and) boost GDP. There’s a national house building programme which he’s already up for. We’ve identified 1.4 million homes on brownfield land.
“Similarly, a national solar rooftop rollout targeting five million public sector homes knocking four or 500 quid off the energy bills for some of the people who have the least money in our country.
“The last one is tax reform, increase the personal allowance and put back what’s been taken away by successive governments through freezing the allowance and we can help the poorest 20% of our population.”
When speaking to Sky News' Sophy Ridge just outside 10 Downing Street, Vince said he was 'overwhelmingly positive' about the new PM
"I am overwhelmingly positive and excited about the changes about to come." he said.
Speaking without the lectern used by his predecessors, Mr Burnham said he would set out a ten-year plan later this year, and, starting on Tuesday, measures to address the cost-of-living squeeze and give people “breathing space now”.
In his first promise as Prime Minister, he said he would “end rough sleeping in our country”. Just hours before his maiden speech, he visited the homelessness charity The Passage in London’s Victoria.
Mr Burnham, who was met with cheers by supporters in Downing Street, said: “I am acutely conscious that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street, the seventh prime minister since 2016, making this a moment for reflection and new resolution.
“It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge.
“Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again.”
The Labour leader pledged to “make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain” – the biggest transformation in the last 40 years, with “a new political model and a new economic model”

sources.text:
Andy Burnham formally became Britain’s new prime minister on Monday, replacing Keir Starmer after a Labour Party revolt and entering Downing Street with promises of sweeping economic change and a tougher approach toward Israel.
The 56-year-old former mayor of Greater Manchester, widely known as the “King of the North,” received his appointment from King Charles III at Buckingham Palace before traveling to 10 Downing Street, where he delivered his first address to the country.
Burnham is Britain’s seventh prime minister in a decade, another sign of the political instability that has gripped the country since the Brexit referendum. He acknowledged the public’s frustration with the rapid turnover of leaders and pledged to rebuild confidence in the government.
“I know people at home are fed up with politics,” Burnham said, speaking without notes and forgoing the lectern traditionally used by incoming prime ministers. “I hear you, and I want to be honest with you: We have not been good enough and we need to be better. We will be.”
He promised to make his arrival a “circuit-breaker for Britain” and said his government would introduce the country’s most significant political and economic changes in four decades.
Burnham said he would present immediate measures aimed at easing the cost-of-living crisis, followed later this year by a 10-year national plan. His domestic agenda includes greater public control over water, electricity and transportation services, increased public investment, expanded housing and mental health services and an effort to revive British industry.
But his rise is also expected to produce a shift in British foreign policy, particularly toward Israel.
Burnham said shortly before taking office that Britain should increase pressure on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and consider additional sanctions over the war in Gaza, violence in the West Bank and the continued expansion of settlements.
In an interview with The Guardian last week, he apologized for Labour’s initial response to the Gaza war, saying the party had been wrong in the early months of the conflict, when Starmer resisted demands for an immediate cease-fire.
Burnham described the suffering of Gaza’s residents as “a scar on our collective conscience” and said the British government had not done enough to pressure Israel.
He stopped short of accusing Israel of genocide, despite demands from parts of Labour’s left wing and pro-Palestinian campaign groups. Burnham said there was “growing evidence” that war crimes had been committed, but argued that any formal determination should be left to international courts.
Burnham said Britain should examine further sanctions against those allegedly involved in violence in Gaza, as well as measures targeting trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
“That is why we need to do more, which includes looking at further sanctions, both on those involved in violence in Gaza, but also looking at steps to ban trade in goods with illegal settlements,” he said.
British Foreign Office officials are already examining possible ways to block goods and services originating in settlements from entering Britain without disrupting what officials describe as legitimate trade with Israel, according to The Guardian.
The new prime minister also criticized the sharp rise in settler violence in the West Bank and East Jerusalem and accused Netanyahu’s government of seeking to make a two-state solution impossible.
His government is expected to face pressure from Labour lawmakers and pro-Palestinian activists to suspend all arms exports to Israel, including British-made components used in the international F-35 fighter jet program.
Britain previously restricted some arms export licenses to Israel under Starmer, but continued permitting the transfer of F-35 components on the grounds that excluding Israel from the multinational supply chain could jeopardize the wider aircraft program.
Burnham may also be pushed to reconsider the previous government’s decision to outlaw Palestine Action as a terrorist organization. Starmer’s government banned the anti-Israel group after a series of break-ins, vandalism incidents and attacks on defense-related facilities.
Burnham did not mention Israel in his first Downing Street speech. He said his first calls to foreign leaders would be to U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and promised there would be no change in Britain’s support for Ukraine.
The omission reflected his immediate focus on domestic affairs, but his earlier remarks indicate that Israel will quickly become one of the most politically contentious issues facing his government.
Anti-Israel demonstrators gathered in London over the weekend demanding that Burnham impose sanctions and take a more confrontational position toward Jerusalem. Signs urged him to “end the genocide” and called for an immediate halt to British military cooperation with Israel.
Burnham’s position places him to the left of Starmer, though he remains more moderate than Labour’s former leader Jeremy Corbyn and others on the party’s hard left.
He is generally associated with Labour’s “soft left,” supporting greater public ownership and higher government investment while avoiding some of the more radical positions identified with Corbyn’s leadership.
Burnham rose to power after Starmer was forced to step down in the face of a rebellion by Labour lawmakers alarmed by the party’s collapse in opinion polls and the growing popularity of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
Starmer, who led Labour to a landslide general election victory in July 2024, delivered a farewell address outside Downing Street before formally submitting his resignation to the king.
“My work is done,” Starmer said, describing his time as prime minister as “the privilege of my life.”
“I leave in good spirits, I leave with a smile and I leave proud of everything we have achieved,” he added, offering Burnham his full support.
Burnham returned to Parliament last month by winning a special election in a seat vacated by an ally. He was then selected as Labour leader without a contested leadership election after no rival entered the race.
Of Labour’s 403 lawmakers, 379 supported his candidacy. Since Labour holds a majority in the 650-seat House of Commons, his election as party leader automatically made him prime minister without a general election.
Opposition parties have argued that Burnham lacks a public mandate for the far-reaching reforms he is proposing. Britain’s next general election must be held by 2029, and Burnham has resisted calls to hold an earlier vote.
His supporters believe his relative popularity, informal style and political profile in northern England give Labour a better chance of stopping Reform UK from winning the next election.
A June YouGov poll found that 34% of Britons had a positive view of Burnham and 38% viewed him negatively, giving him a net rating of minus four points. While still negative, it was far stronger than Starmer’s rating of minus 45 and Farage’s minus 40.
Burnham built much of his reputation during nine years as mayor of Greater Manchester, where he repeatedly challenged the central government in London and advocated greater authority for northern regions.
As prime minister, he has promised to decentralize power and establish a second working base in Manchester, which he has called “10 Downing Street North.”
His economic program represents another break with the Starmer era. Burnham has blamed decades of privatization and what he describes as neoliberal economic policy for rising costs, declining services and the concentration of political power in London.
He wants stronger public control of rail, bus, water and energy services, though it remains unclear whether this would involve full nationalization in every sector or tighter government regulation of privately operated companies.
He said the initial measures would provide Britons with “breathing space” as the government addresses housing costs, welfare spending, unemployment and stagnant living standards.
Burnham is also expected to adopt a more pragmatic position on oil and natural gas drilling in the North Sea, drawing praise from Trump.
Trump claimed in a post on Truth Social that residents of Aberdeen were “dancing in the streets” because Burnham planned to open Britain’s offshore oil resources.
“They are dancing in the streets!” Trump wrote, arguing that increased drilling could transform Britain from an economically struggling country into one of the richest in the world.
It remains unclear how many new drilling projects Burnham will approve. The BBC reported that he is expected to remain formally committed to Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which opposed new exploration licenses, while allowing development in areas where permits have already been granted.
Burnham must also appoint his Cabinet, including a finance minister who will be responsible for translating his promises into a credible spending and taxation program. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is considered a leading candidate for the Treasury post.
Conservative opposition leader Kemi Badenoch warned Burnham against raising taxes and accused him of entering office without a clear plan.
“You must not repeat the mistakes of Keir Starmer’s premiership,” she wrote in an open letter, urging him to resist pressure from Labour’s left wing for higher welfare spending.
Burnham’s first months in office will therefore be dominated by the cost of living, public services and Labour’s struggle against Reform UK. But his comments before taking power also suggest that Britain’s relationship with Israel could soon face another period of strain.
Any decision to expand sanctions, restrict settlement trade, halt arms exports or reverse the ban on Palestine Action would deepen tensions with Jerusalem and mark a clear departure from Starmer’s more cautious approach.
For now, Burnham has promised immediate domestic action and a long-term transformation of Britain. On Israel, however, the direction is already becoming apparent: more pressure, closer scrutiny and the possibility of additional punitive measures.

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham promises to bring back ‘hope’ to Britain as he becomes Prime Minister
sources.text:
ANDY Burnham has become Prime Minister after accepting the King’s invitation to form a Government, pledging to restore public faith in politics and bring “hope” back to Britain.
In his first speech outside Number 10 Downing Street, Mr Burnham acknowledged the political instability of recent years and said his administration would seek to deliver both political and economic reform.
The new Prime Minister noted that he was the sixth person in a decade to take office at Downing Street and the seventh prime minister since 2016, describing the moment as one requiring “reflection and new resolution”.
Mr Burnham said politicians needed to “raise our game and rise to the new challenge”, arguing that Britain must show it can regain stability and restore confidence in democratic institutions.
Acknowledging public frustration with Westminster, he said: “I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you and I want to be honest with you – we have not been good enough, and we need to be better.”
He promised what he described as a “circuit breaker for Britain”, saying his Government would bring forward “the biggest changes in the last 40 years” through a new political model and a new economic model.
The Prime Minister criticised aspects of Britain’s economic and political direction since the 1980s, arguing that power had become too centralised and that many communities affected by deindustrialisation had been left behind.
Mr Burnham pledged to devolve more power from Westminster, saying his Government would “take power out of here, and carry it into every postcode in the land”. He also said he wanted to build “a new economy” and put “life’s essentials back under stronger public control” while using public procurement to support British industry.
He announced plans to publish a 10-year plan for Britain later this year, setting out a long-term vision for the country.
The Prime Minister also signalled early action on living costs, saying he would outline measures to give people “some breathing space” and provide help with the cost of living.
Among his priorities, Mr Burnham said the Government would help more young people into work through changes to the education system, increased mental health support and the construction of more council homes.
He said those measures would help reduce welfare spending “in a fair and sustainable way” while allowing the Government to meet its fiscal rules and defence commitments.
Mr Burnham also pledged to build what he described as a more preventative state, focused on supporting people before problems become crises.
Setting out his first priority in office, he said: “I will soon go through that door behind me and issue my first instruction to end rough sleeping in our country.”
Concluding his address, the Prime Minister called for unity and optimism, urging the public to help build “a new national sense of unity, of common purpose, and positivity”.
He added: “Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again, the moment we bring back hope.”
Burnham said these measures would help reduce welfare spending in a "fair and sustainable" way while allowing the government to maintain its fiscal rules and defence commitments.
He also signalled a significant shift in public services, promising a more preventative approach focused on intervention and support rather than crisis management.
One of his first acts as Prime Minister, he said, would be to issue instructions aimed at ending rough sleeping.
"I will soon go through that door behind me and issue my first instruction to end rough sleeping in our country," he told the nation.
Ending his address, Burnham called for national unity and a renewed sense of optimism after years of political division.
"Let's build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose, and positivity," he said.
"Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again, the moment we bring back hope."
The speech marks the beginning of a premiership that appears set to be defined by devolution, state intervention in key services and an attempt to recast the relationship between Westminster and Britain's regions.
