Andy Burnham Becomes UK's 7th Prime Minister in a Decade
sources.text:
Andy Burnham is officially Britain's new prime minister. Burnham formally accepted an invitation from King Charles III to form a government, reports the AP, with Buckingham Palace releasing a photo of the two men shaking hands. The ceremony, known as "kissing hands," marks the transfer of power from former leader Keir Starmer to Burnham. Burnham replaced Starmer as leader of the center-left governing Labour Party last week. He is the seventh UK prime minister since 2016 in a now well-rehearsed handover after replacing Starmer as leader of the center-left governing Labour Party on Friday. 
 
  
                                    
                                    
                                
                                
                             
                            
                            
                            
                            
                            
                                
                                
                                    
                                        
 Starmer made a short farewell speech outside the prime minister's 10 Downing Street residence, saying "my work is done." The outgoing leader, forced to resign by his own party, said Britain is now "stronger and fairer than it was two years ago," when he took office. "I go with good grace, I go with a smile and I go proud of everything that we have achieved," Starmer said before heading to Buckingham Palace to offer his resignation to the king. It was an offer "His Majesty was graciously pleased to accept," the palace said in a statement.
                                    
                                
                                
                                
                                
                                
                                    
                                        Britain's parliamentary democracy allows governing parties to change leaders, and thus prime ministers, without the need for a general election. The next national poll doesn't have to be held until 2029, though Burnham can call one sooner if he wants. From the palace, Burnham will go to Downing Street, where he will make his first speech as prime minister.

sources.news_title: New PM Andy Burnham: Britain must ‘regain our stability’
King Charles Just Appointed Andrew Burnham Prime Minister
sources.text:
King Charles has not even been on the throne for four years and he has now appointed the fourth Prime Minister of his reign. The King received the new leader of the UK’s Labour Party, Andy Burnham, today and invited him to form a government.
“His Majesty received in audience the Rt. Hon. Andrew Burnham MP and requested him to form a new Administration,” Buckingham Palace said in a statement just after midday today. “The Rt. Hon Andrew Burnham MP accepted The King's offer and kissed hands upon his appointment as Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury. Ms. Marie-France van Heel was also received by His Majesty.”
The term “kissed hands” is still used to describe the appointment of a new minister, even though ministers no longer actually kiss the monarch’s hand. Buckingham Palace released an image of the King and Andy Burnham shaking hands today during the meeting.
Today’s appointment was part of a highly orchestrated series of events that saw outgoing Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer visit the King immediately before Andy Burnham to formally tender his resignation. He had announced he was stepping down last month, but stayed on in the post until a new leader was chosen.
“The Rt. Hon. Sir Keir Starmer MP had an audience of The King this morning and tendered his resignation as Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury which His Majesty was graciously pleased to accept,” Buckingham Palace said about that meeting today. “Lady Starmer was also received by The King.”
Both meetings took place in the King’s temporary official audience room, the Chinese Dining Room, as the usual audience room is out of action due to the ongoing Palace renovations.
The meetings today highlight the key constitutional role that the monarch plays during a change of Prime Minister. While the British sovereign no longer has any political power when it comes to legislation, they do still have the personal prerogative to appoint the Prime Minister. This usually happens after a general election, when the monarch invites the winning party’s leader to form a government. But sometimes, as in this case, a Prime Minister resigns between general elections and the King needs to appoint a new one. In this case they must choose someone who can command the confidence of the House of Commons.
As the Labour Party remained in power when Keir Starmer resigned, it was up to them to choose their new leader to become Prime Minister. The party elected Andy Burnham as their leader last Friday.
Burnham is the fourth Prime Minister of the King’s reign following Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak, and Sir Keir Starmer. Starmer holds the title of Sir because he was knighted for his services to criminal justice following his previous role as Director of Public Prosecutions.
Andy Burnham is best known for his previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester, a position he held for almost a decade. He has announced plans for “No. 10 North,” to move part of his office to Manchester.
Town & Country Contributing Editor Victoria Murphy has reported on the British Royal Family since 2010. She has interviewed Prince Harry and has travelled the world covering several royal tours. She is a frequent contributor to Good Morning America. Victoria authored Town & Country book The Queen: A Life in Pictures, released in 2021.

sources.news_title: Seven key promises Andy Burnham's just made now he's Prime Minister
sources.text:
Andy Burnham: 7 key promises he's just made as Prime Minister
Big announcements made on the steps of Downing Street as former Manchester mayor replaces Sir Keir Starmer
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham set out seven key promises in his first speech as Prime Minister. And he also announced a clear direction of travel, condemning the path the UK has taken over the past 40 years.
He was attacking the reforms introduced by Margaret Thatcher’s government in the 1980s, but the comments also sounded like a criticism of later Labour governments for failing to reverse them. Mr Burnham said: “We will make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years – a new political model and a new economic model. In the 1980s, Britain took some wrong turns.”
But he also had an upbeat message, saying: “I will give this my all, and I ask you all to pull with me. Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose, and positivity. Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again, the moment we bring back hope.”
Here are the main announcements from the speech:
Devolving power out of London
The new Prime Minister highlighted plans to make more decisions in regions across the country rather than in Whitehall.
This is expected to mean giving more power to mayors, as well as creating an office for central government, known as No 10 North, in the Manchester region.
Mr Burnham said: “We will take power out of here, and carry it into every postcode in the land, so that they can do more.”
Bringing utilities such as gas and water under greater public control
Mr Burnham will give either central government or regional mayors control over key utilities such as gas, water and electricity.
They are currently privately owned. But he said they will be placed into “public control” rather than public ownership, suggesting they will not be fully nationalised.
He promised to “build a new economy, where we put life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again”.
Making government agencies buy from British firms
Mr Burnham will order public services to “buy British” when possible, to create more jobs in the UK.
He talked about “reindustrialising Britain using public procurement to back British industry”.
Help with the cost of living
The new Prime Minister is aiming to announce measures designed to help people struggling with the cost of living quickly, but has not yet provided details.
He said: “I can do something to give people some breathing space now, some help with the cost of living, and I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them.”
Education and mental health reforms to help struggling young people
Mr Burnham vowed to help young people, after new figures showed a million aged 16 to 24 are not in education, employment or training (known as NEET).
He said: “We will help more young people into work by changing the education system and giving them more support, more mental health support.”
A massive housebuilding programme
Promising more social housing, he said: “We will build more council homes.”
A full policy programme to be announced in the summer
The new Prime Minister warned we will have to wait for fuller details of his plan for the UK.
He said: “Later this year, I will bring forward a new plan for Britain, a 10-year plan, laying out a path from where we are now to where I believe we all want Britain to be, wherever we’re coming from, whatever party we support.”
And other things we know
Although not mentioned in the speech, Mr Burnham’s team have already said he will scrap the digital ID scheme planned by Sir Keir Starmer’s government. There are also reports he will allow more North Sea drilling.

sources.news_title: Why Britain is getting a new prime minister without a general election
sources.text:
By — Sylvia Hui, Associated Press Sylvia Hui, Associated Press Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/why-britain-is-getting-a-new-prime-minister-without-a-general-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Why Britain is getting a new prime minister without a general election World Jul 20, 2026 8:32 AM EDT LONDON (AP) — Veteran Labour Party politician and popular former Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham has become Britain's next prime minister, formally taking over Monday from Keir Starmer, who announced his resignation last month. Burnham was the only candidate to secure enough support from his fellow Labour lawmakers to replace Starmer as leader of the governing party. Because Labour holds a majority in government, its leader also becomes the U.K. prime minister. Burnham received support from 379 out of 401 Labour Party lawmakers, and was announced Labour leader at a special party conference on Friday. He officially became prime minister on Monday, when he met King Charles III at Buckingham Palace for a formal go-ahead. A look at how and why Britain is getting a new prime minister just two years after Starmer led his party to a landslide election victory: Why is there a change of leader without a general election? Britain's parliamentary democracy allows governing parties to change leaders midterm, with the winner becoming prime minister without the need for a general election. Prime ministers can be replaced if one has resigned as leader of their party, or been forced out by a leadership challenge. The next national election does not have to be held until 2029, five years from the last election in 2024. Starmer announced he was quitting as Labour leader on June 22 after barely two years in power, ending a tenure marred by a series of political missteps — most notably his decision to appoint a man with close ties to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein as Britain's ambassador to the United States. Heavy losses suffered by Labour in a midterm set of local elections in May prompted many lawmakers to demand Starmer's resignation. And when Burnham — favored by many within Labour to lead the party and the country — won a special election for a seat in Parliament, Starmer gave in to the mounting pressure to quit. His resignation automatically triggered a Labour leadership contest. Under Labour rules, a lawmaker can challenge the leader if they have the backing of a fifth of the party's House of Commons lawmakers. There was no contestant other than Burnham, who comfortably surpassed that threshold. Burnham is the seventh prime minister in a decade It's not unusual for prime ministers to come to power without a broad election under Britain's parliamentary system. In fact, four of the six British prime ministers in the past decade took the top job by winning internal party leadership contests to replace their predecessors, not by public vote. READ MORE: How Brexit broke British politics In the 2010s, both Theresa May and Boris Johnson became prime minister after winning Conservative leadership races when their predecessors resigned midterm. When Johnson announced he was quitting in 2022, the Conservatives held a leadership contest and the party's members chose Liz Truss to replace him. And when Truss stepped down, just 49 days later, she was in turn replaced by Rishi Sunak via a similar process. Burnham thus becomes the seventh prime minister in a turbulent decade of U.K. politics, marked by a rapid succession of leaders who all, to some extent, failed to successfully manage the messy aftermath of Britain's decision to divorce from the European Union. Power changes hands in a well-rehearsed ritual Britain's newly appointed Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel greet supporters as they arrive at 10 Downing Street for Burnham's first day in office on Monday. Photo by Temilade Adelaja/Reuters After years of leadership churn, the sequence of traditional events involved in the transfer of power has become familiar for many in Britain. On Monday, Starmer made his farewell speech to the public before going to Buckingham Palace to hold a short meeting with the king and formally resign. Then it was Burnham's turn to arrive at the palace, where Charles formally asked him to form a government. The private meeting is known as the "Kissing of Hands," in accordance with historic tradition, though no hands are actually kissed and the men are more likely to shake hands. When Burnham left the palace he became the 59th person to hold the office of British prime minister. The whole sequence is typically broadcast live on television — and is over within hours. sources.news_title: Andy Burnham appointed Britain's new prime minister
sources.text:
Andy Burnham was sworn in as the United Kingdom’s new prime minister, taking over from the historically unpopular Keir Starmer.
The former Manchester mayor has taken the country’s top elected office just four weeks after entering parliament, having been floated as Starmer’s most likely successor since his premiership entered its existential danger phase earlier this year. Burnham became prime minister after a meeting with King Charles III in Buckingham Palace, as per U.K. procedure, shortly after the king accepted Starmer’s resignation. A statement from Buckingham Palace said the king had “requested him to form a new Administration.”
Recommended Stories
The Labour Party leader “accepted The King’s offer and kissed hands upon his appointment as Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury.”
BURNHAM ‘FINALIZING’ CABINET PICKS AHEAD OF APPOINTMENT AS UK PRIME MINISTER
The appointment is a historic one — Burnham is the first Catholic to lead the country since the death of Queen Mary Tudor in 1558, in a country that long distinguished itself in its opposition to Catholicism. Catholics were long persecuted and barred from office, and some laws still in the books barring certain Catholic influence may trigger some awkwardness.
Hopes are high within Labour that Burnham can revive their fortunes, after repeated scandals and record low popularity. The new prime minister has projected an image of vigor, claiming the party’s problems can be traced back to its departure from its founding philosophy. He has pledged to refocus the party on the working class, public-private cooperation economically, and a boost in social spending.
This message was central in his first speech as prime minister outside 10 Downing Street, promising that his premiership would be a “circuit breaker” for the U.K., “bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years.”
“Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again, and that is our challenge: to make politics work, to make it work better,” Burnham said, admitting that, “We have not been good enough, and we need to be better. We will be.”
He bemoaned the “wrong turns” the country had made since the 1980s.
“Political power was centralized, economic power privatized,” Burnham said. “Large parts of the country deindustrialized, and they still haven’t recovered. Many feel as though they’re still in decline, and they don’t have the ability to turn things around. And that’s why we will change politics to make it more collaborative, more about problem solving than point scoring.”
Starmer pledged his full support to his successor in his own final speech in the same spot less than an hour before.
EUROPE’S DEMOGRAPHIC TIME BOMB IS KILLING ITS LEADERS’ POPULARITY
“He has my full support,” Starmer said. “I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything we have achieved.”
Though Burnham’s taking of the reins has sparked a groundswell of hope from Labour members, he faces major challenges. The U.K.’s six prime ministers since Brexit have all left office despised, largely due to structural economic issues associated with an aging population. His peers in Western Europe have failed to overcome these issues and now grapple with some of the lowest approval ratings in their respective histories.
The fall of Starmer
Burnham’s rise directly coincided with Starmer’s fall, as the now-former prime minister was able to resist pressure to bow out until the popular Burnham’s by-election victory in the constituency of Makerfield. Burnham had been out of parliament since 2017, serving as the Mayor of Greater Manchester.
Starmer also entered office with high hopes, after Labour crushed its Tory rivals in an electoral landslide in the summer of 2024. His honeymoon lasted only a few weeks, with his first of many crises being the handling of the U.K.’s Winter Fuel Payment, a subsidy paid to pensioners since 1997.
Just weeks after taking office, his Chancellor Rachel Reeves announced that the subsidy was being narrowed from all 11.6 million pensioners to around 1.5 million who met special criteria. It was acknowledged as a “tough choice” that Reeves “didn’t want to make, or expected to make,” but the rising deficit made it a needed fix.
Couching the move with a preemptively apologetic statement didn’t satiate the rage of pensioners and the public, who savaged Starmer’s government in the press. Critics didn’t shy away from directly accusing Starmer’s government of essentially killing pensioners. Despite rolling the reform back in the spring, the damage had already been done, and Starmer’s popularity never recovered. The Telegraph credited the saga as sealing Starmer’s fate.
“If headlines of freezing grannies dominate the first year of your premiership, it may not be destined for greatness,” Telegraph senior money writer Maya Wilson Autzen wrote.
The misstep would prove to be only the first of many. Starmer appointed Lord Peter Mandelson ambassador to the U.S. in February 2025, then fired him in September after his relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein came to light. The trickle of documents concerning Epstein was released over several months at the urging of U.S. lawmakers, ensuring the scandal would remain in British headlines for months.
The worst batch of correspondence between Epstein and Mandelson was released in late January, including emails indicating that he received approximately $75,000 from Epstein and offered the convicted sex trafficker insights on political affairs while serving in former Prime Minister Gordon Brown’s Cabinet. Epstein also made multiple payments to Mandelson’s romantic partner, and a photo emerged showing Mandelson without pants interacting with a woman whose identity was redacted. The first surge of calls for Starmer to resign coincided with these releases in January.
Starmer struggled to handle the scandal and was forced to admit that the government was aware of Mandelson’s association when he was appointed, but decided to go through with it anyway.
While the Mandelson affair was the most high-profile killer, Starmer’s inability to turn the U.K.’s stagnating economy around was the main culprit. Successive governments have been crippled by chronic economic stagnation and an inability to lower the cost of living. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and ensuing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz had a disproportionate impact on the U.K. and obliterated any chances of a quick recovery.
The writing on the wall became evident on May 7, when Labour suffered an electoral bloodbath in the country’s local elections. Labour lost more than 1,100 seats that it began the day with, winning just over 1,000 seats that were up for grabs. It lost control of Wales after a century in power, and saw its worst turnout yet in the Scottish elections.
By May 11, more than 60 Labour MPs called upon Starmer to resign. Four Parliamentary private secretaries, junior members of the government, resigned and used the opportunity to call upon Starmer to step down. The prime minister had accepted responsibility for the May 7 losses but vowed to hold on in a May 11 speech.
By the time of his resignation, Starmer had made history as the island nation’s most unpopular premier, with an Ipsos poll finding just 13% of voters were satisfied with him, compared to 79% who were unsatisfied.
Labour’s last hope
The unenviable task of handling all of these lingering issues now falls to Burnham. The new leader said he was “acutely conscious” of the scale of the task before him in his first speech.
Wary of the main issue that sunk his predecessor, Burnham focused much of his first speech on affordability, saying his government would “build a new economy, where we put life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again, reindustrializing Britain using public procurement to back British industry.”
He promised to put forward a 10-year plan for the U.K.
Burnham also touched on his signature approach of decentralization, delegating more power to local governments, as was his approach as mayor of Manchester.
Part of Labour’s hope in Burnham lies in his broader popularity. He’s one of the most popular politicians in the country, but in an indictment of U.K. politics, this high approval rating stands at just 34% as of June, according to a YouGov poll, with a -4 point net approval rating. The same poll had Starmer at -45.
Burnham’s popularity within the party also has to do with his handling of dissent. Starmer was known for his intolerance of diverging voices within the party, while Burnham has pledged to listen to backbenchers. He is also viewed as having an intellectual foundation for his overhaul of the party, working closely with Labour adjacent think tanks such as Common Wealth, the New Economics Foundation, and the Institute for Public Policy Research.
His unique, decentralized approach and wider perception of a fresh approach to Labor have given rise to hope within the party that he could revive the party in a new direction in time for the next elections.
Whatever his challenges, Burnham has a fair amount of time to change the direction of the country. The Labor Party is not required to call a new general election until 2029.
This is a breaking news story and may be updated.

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham promises to build 'national unity' in first speech as Prime Minister
sources.text:
Andy Burnham has promised "to build a national sense of unity" in the UK as he became the seventh Prime Minister in a decade today after Sir Keir Starmer’s resignation.
In his first speech as Prime Minister after meeting the King at Buckingham Palace, Mr Burnham pledged to build a new economy and underlined his ambition for greater devolution of power from Westminster saying he wished to deliver power to "every postcode".
Speaking outside Number 10 watched by his wife Marie-France van Heel, he vowed to help tackle the cost of liviing and to get more young people into work.
He also promised to win over voters “fed up with politics” and "show the world" that the UK can once again be a source of stability.
Read More:
- Indyref2: Andy Burnham rules out new vote on independence
- Burnham to take 'more pragmatic' stance to North Sea
- Andy Burnham to become seventh UK Prime Minister in a decade
- Who is Andy Burnham’s wife Marie-France van Heel?
Delivering his speech without the lectern used by his predecessors, he said he would set out help to build more council houses, and that his first instruction on entering Number 10 would be to “end rough sleeping in our country”.
Mr Burnham, who was met with cheers by supporters in Downing Street, said: “I am acutely conscious that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street, the seventh prime minister since 2016, making this a moment for reflection and new resolution.
“It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge.
“Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again.”
The Labour leader pledged to “make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain”, with the biggest transformation in the last 40 years.
He made no mention of Scotland or the other devolved nations in his speech.
Mr Burnham said: “We will change politics, to make it more collaborative, more about problem solving than point-scoring, and will take power out of here and carry it into every postcode in the land, so that they can do more, and in doing more, build a new economy where we put life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again, reindustrialising Britain using public procurement to back British industry.”
With many seeing Britain as deeply divided economically, and the devolved administrations all led by parties that want to leave the UK, he concluded his first speech as Prime Minister by urging people to “pull with me” to “build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity”.
He said: "I will put the care of people at the heart of everything I do. I will give this my all, and I ask you all to pull with me.
"Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity. Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again. The moment we bring back hope."
Earlier Mr Burnham told The Times that “frustration” about a five-year-long freeze in the £12,570 limit on how much can be earned before paying income tax had “lodged in my mind” during his campaign to win the Makerfield by-election.
“They’re just characterising me as a tax raiser,” he said. “Well, again, it’s never that simplistic, is it?”
Mr Burnham became Prime Minister after “kissing hands” with the King – the private ceremony by which he accepts the invitation to form a government.
First Minister John Swinney congratulated Mr Burnham on his appointment as Prime Minister and repeated his call for discussions on a second independence referendum. Earlier this month Mr Burnham told Scottish Labour MPs he would not agree to a new vote.
“I congratulate Andy Burnham on his appointment as Prime Minister," said Mr Swinney.
"This is a significant moment for the United Kingdom, and I commit to working constructively with him in order to improve the lives of people in Scotland.
“The UK faces a number of serious challenges at this moment, and Andy Burnham is correct when he says that Westminster is not working for the vast majority of people.
“Therefore, taking action on the cost of living must be an absolute priority for the new Prime Minister, and supporting people through sustained economic pressures will be key to restoring confidence and stability after a period of political turbulence.
“Just two months ago, the people of Scotland voted for my Government and our commitment to support people with the cost of living, ensure easier and quicker access to the NHS, and deliver the right to choose a fresh start with independence.
“I look forward to constructive conversations with the new Prime Minister about how we make that happen.”
Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar said: “Congratulations to Andy Burnham on becoming Prime Minister.
“I am confident that Andy will rise to the challenge he has set out today - to make our politics better, to make sure it works for people and delivers the change our country so desperately needs.
“We must re-empower those communities that have been forgotten about and left behind, and re-industrialise every part of our great country.
“That is what we can expect from this Labour government, taking on the poison of Reform and bringing hope back to Britain.”
Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay called for the new Prime Minister to end the UK Government ban on new North Sea drilling.
On Sunday, Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell said Mr Burnham would take "a more pragmatic approach" to North Sea gas and oil - prompting US President Donald Trump to say people in Aberdeen will be "dancing in the streets".
Mr Findlay said: “Labour’s decision to boot Sir Keir Starmer out of 10 Downing Street changes absolutely nothing.
“Andy Burnham is just a new frontman for a failing left-wing government that hates aspiration, splurges vast sums of taxpayers’ money on benefits and doesn’t take our national security seriously.
“Unless Burnham rejects net zero zealots Ed Miliband’s idiotic ban on new North Sea drilling, 1,000 jobs every month will continue to be lost and the industry will be destroyed.
“With Burnham supporting many of the SNP’s disastrous left-wing policies, Scots face a double whammy of pain and misery.
“The people of Scotland deserve better than two out-of-touch governments who are intent on wrecking our economy and risking our energy security.”
The carefully choreographed handover of power came after Sir Keir had his own audience with Charles to resign formally.
Before heading to the Palace, Sir Keir said “my work is done” and “I go with a smile” in his final speech in front of his wife Lady Victoria Starmer, colleagues and friends in Downing Street.
His final exit from No 10 was quieter than when he announced he would be resigning as a Metropolitan Police ban prevented protesters including anti-Brexit campaigner Steve Bray from playing loud music outside Downing Street to drown out his words.
Sir Keir said: “I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything that we have achieved.”

sources.news_title: Meet the New Boss: Andy Burnham Installed as UK Prime Minister
sources.text:
Veteran Westminster swamp creature turned ‘King of the North’ political chameleon Andy Burnham has been given the keys to Number 10 Downing Street, officially taking over the office of Prime Minister on Monday after Sir Keir Starmer was forced to resign just over two years after taking power.
The London political churn has spat out another one. Sir Keir Starmer formally resigned as Prime Minister to make way for former Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham, who became the seventh prime minister in a decade, and fifth to take power in less than four years. While Burnham presents as a more personable figure than his predecessor, it remains to be seen how far northern charm will take him and if he can deliver on the key priorities of the British public.
Starmer attempted to hold his head high on Monday morning as he left Downing Street — as opposed to the tearful resignation announcement he delivered last month — claiming that he left the country in a “stronger and fairer” position than it was when he came into office. This was clearly not the opinion of the British public, who delivered Starmer’s Labour Party an electoral drubbing in the local ‘mid-term’ elections in May in favour of Brexit boss Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party.
The defeat came in the wake of his government failing to return the British economy to growth while imposing the highest tax burden on the nation since the Second World War and having failed to protect the country’s borders, with over 70,000 illegals crossing the English Channel under his watch, the most of any modern prime minister.
The Starmer government was marred from the start, having bungled the response to the Southport massacre, in which he appeared to have more rage toward the so-called “far-right” rioters than towards the Rwandan-heritage teen who stabbed three young girls to death and left ten more injured at a Taylor Swift dance party just days into his term. However, the drumbeat call for his resignation truly ramped up last autumn following the release of the Epstein files by the Trump administration in the United States, which revealed that Starmer’s ambassador to Washington, Peter ‘Prince of Darkness’ Mandelson, had continued his close relationship with the New York financier long after he was convicted of his first child prostitution offence.
Sir Keir attempted to limp on, throwing his longtime political ally, Chief of Staff, and architect of his rise, Morgan McSweeney, to the wolves. Yet his continued presence as Prime Minister appeared more of a function of no challenger being foolish to take over the job — and therefore the blame — before the expected heavy losses at the May elections, shortly after which self-described socialist Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham finally put himself forward for the top job.
This morning, Burnham met with King Charles III for the traditional “kissing hands” ceremony, in which the British Monarch officially invited Burnham to form a government in his name.
In his first address to the nation as Prime Minister outside Number 10, Burnham acknowledged the political turmoil that led to his rise, saying: “I am acutely conscious that I am… the seventh Prime Minister since 2016. Making this a moment for reflection, and new resolution… it requires my generation of politicians to raise our game, and rise to the challenge. Britain needs to show the world we can regain our stability once again.”
In his speech, the new PM pitched himself as an economic reformer, promising to bring prosperity from London to the rest of the country.
“We will take power out of here and carry it into every postcode in the land, so that they can do more, and in doing more, build a new economy where we put life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again,” he said.
Despite his folksy act, having taken the moniker of ‘King of the North’, following his nearly decade in office as the Mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham appeared to have consciously concocted such an image after spending the prior decade as a Westminster insider under the governments of former Labour PMs Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.
His rise to the highest office in the land over the past month also had the distinct odour of swamp. To put forward a leadership challenge against Starmer, Burnham needed a seat in the House of Commons, and the constituency of Makerfield was conveniently vacated by anti-Breitbart activist MP Josh Simons, who himself had been forced out of the Starmer government over scandals involving his pro-censorship activities at the Labour Together think tank founded by Starmer’s former Chief of Staff Morgan McSweeney.
Simons, who appeared outside of Downing Street on Monday morning’s coronation for Burnham, is tipped to be set for a top gig in the new government in exchange for his move to give up his seat in Makerfield for the new PM. His return to power will likely signal continued crackdowns on social media, potentially including a ban on VPNs, as the government seeks to ban under-16s from accessing social media.
Burnham’s victory in Makerfield last month was also facilitated, in part, by the help of the far-left cancel culture group HOPE Not Hate, which busied itself with digging up old social media posts of Burnham’s Reform opponent, and allegedly even leafleting on behalf of the Labour Party, for which Nigel Farage has launched a complaint at the Electoral Commission. Nevertheless, with just over 25,000 votes, Burnham was sent to Parliament and enabled to become Prime Minister.
Yet, without having run on the 2024 Labour Party manifesto and only having been backed by a mere fraction of the public, Burnham is already facing calls for a general election from Farage and others, who argue that his administration has no popular mandate to govern.
Burnham does not appear to have any interest in fighting a general election; indeed, he promised a Soviet-style 10-year plan to fix Britain’s economy, which he claimed was only faltering as a result of the policies put in place by Margaret Thatcher over four decades ago.
“We have not been good enough and we need to be better. We will be. We will make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in 40 years. A new political model, and a new economic model. In the 1980s, Britain took some wrong turns. Political power was centralised, economic power privatised. Large parts of the country, deindustrialised.”
He vowed to “build a new economy where we put life’s essentials under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again. Reindustrialising Britain again with public procurement to back British industry. Later this year I will bring forward a new Plan for Britain. A ten year plan.”
Burnham vowed to bring down the cost of living, build more state housing, end homeless sleeping, reform the education system with more mental health support, and claimed that he would reduce welfare spending while meeting international defence commitments.
Yet with details lacking on Monday and his new government already signalling against new energy extraction from the oil-rich North Sea, it remains to be seen how such an industrial plan will fare. Urging his new counterpart in London to adopt his “drill baby, drill” ethos, U.S. President Trump urged Burnham to take advantage of Britain’s natural resources in the North Sea, saying that it could transform the UK from a “Poverty Stricken Disaster, to one of the Richest Countries anywhere in the World!”
Time will tell if this Prime Minister will actually listen to such advice from across the pond, or if it will be more of the same from Burnham.

sources.news_title: 'Andy Burnham calls time on the gloominess of the past as he backs hope'
sources.text:
Andy Burnham’s Downing Street address was a tale of two Julys.
When Keir Starmer became Prime Minister in July 2024, his Government announced a so-called £22bn black hole in the finances.
It was linked to a series of cuts, including to the winter fuel payment, that were deeply unpopular with voters.
Starmer’s gloomy tone misjudged the mood of the public and he never recovered.
Burnham, a more skilled politician than his predecessor, did not make this mistake in July 2026.
He not only explicitly promised an end to a failing status quo, but an end to the economic model of the past forty years, even though this included the New Labour years.
He also dispensed with the early hairshirt approach of Starmer by backing a “new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity”.
Today, he claimed, would be a "circuit breaker" for the country.
Where Starmer’s Government focused on taking money away from voters, Burnham is also focused on giving people “breathing room” from the cost of living crisis.
Starmer was about pain and Burnham focused on gain.
The new PM’s fresh approach will continue throughout the summer, free of the shackles of Westminster scrutiny.
His UK tour will attempt to build a sense of hope and positivity in a country that has been lacking in both.
He will announce a suite of feel-good announcements to show he is on the side of hard-pressed citizens.
Much of the commentary so far has portrayed Burnham as a 1970s-style socialist wanting to jack up taxes.
He may increase taxes where there is unfairness in the system, but every indication is he wants to go in the opposite direction.
He has spoken about lifting the tax free personal allowance for income tax - a tax cut in all but name for workers and pensioners.
Taking the edge off energy bills, perhaps through abolishing VAT, would also make voters better off.
People across the UK have been told for sixteen years that they must tighten their belts to pay down debt and close deficits.
Burnham’s speech is an early sign he wants to turn the corner on the miserablism of Westminster politics by going in the opposite direction.

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham's speech in full - 'moment Britain starts to believe again'
sources.text:
Andy Burnham's speech in full - new PM sets out 'moment Britain starts to believe again'
Speaking outside No10, new Prime Minister Andy Burnham vowed to set out a 10-year plan and bring in new measures to give people 'breathing space' with the cost of living
Andy Burnham has pledged to set out a 10-year plan to change Britain as he set out what he described as "the moment when Britain starts to believe again".
Speaking outside No10, the new Prime Minister said his first action would be to set out a plan to end rough sleeping. And he promised to announce measures to tackle the cost of living in the coming days.
Mr Burnham, who returned to Parliament last month having been the Mayor of Greater Manchester for nearly a decade, admitted voters had been failed by politicians. He said the churn of Prime Ministers requires the government to "raise our game".
He said: "We will make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years."
Andy Burnham's speech in full
"I have just come from Buckingham Palace, where I have accepted His Majesty the King's invitation to form a government. In doing so, I am acutely conscious that I am the sixth person in the last ten years to walk up this street, the seventh Prime Minister since 2016 - making this a moment for reflection and new resolution.
"It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge. Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again, and that is our challenge - to make politics work, to make it work better.
"I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you and I want to be honest with you, we have not been good enough and we need to be better. We will be.
"We will make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years.
"A new political model and a new economic model. In the 1980s, Britain took some wrong turns. Political power was centralised, economic power privatised large parts of the country deindustrialised, and they still haven't recovered.
"Many feel as though they're still in decline, and they don't have the ability to turn things around. And that's why we will change politics, to make it more collaborative, more about problem-solving than point scoring.
"And we will take power out of here and carry it into every postcode in the land so that they can do more and in doing more, build a new economy where we put life's essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again.
"Re-industrializing Britain using public procurement to back British industry.
"Later this year I will bring forward a new plan for Britain, a ten year plan laying out a path from where we are now to where I believe we all want Britain to be, wherever we're coming from, whatever party we support.
"But I can do something to give people some breathing space now, some help with the cost of living. And I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them.
"We will help more young people into work by changing the education system and giving them more support, more mental health support, and we will build more council homes.
"That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down to meet our fiscal rules and to honor our commitments on defense to our international partners.
"We will help people to live well, building a more preventative state, investing in people's success rather than paying for failure. And that work starts now.
"I will soon go through that door behind me and issue my first instruction to end rough sleeping in our country. It's about putting the right values and the right standards at the heart of government.
"I will put the care of people at the heart of everything I do. I will give this my all, and I ask you all to pull with me.
"Let's build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity. Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again, the moment we bring back hope. Thank you very much, everybody."

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham becomes UK's next prime minister after meeting with King Charles III
Andy Burnham officially becomes UK’s prime minister
Burnham becomes UK’s new PM after meeting King Charles
sources.text:
Starmer departed Downing Street on Monday morning, insisting in a farewell speech his two years in office had made Britain a better place.
The monarch met Starmer to accept his resignation, and Burnham arrived next for the formal procedure in which he asked him to form the next government and he accepted.
Starmer, 56, was the sixth prime minister to enter Downing Street in the last 10 years.
“I am confident that Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago,” he told reporters in his farewell speech outside his central London office.
“I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything that we have achieved.”
Burnham will face an in-tray overflowing with challenges with little time to make his mark.
In an interview with The Times published late Sunday, he said he wanted to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil.
“What we’ve been doing hasn’t been working. That’s the way I see it.
“I am going to try and do things in a different way,” he said.
In his first speech, Burnham will set out “priorities for restoring confidence in government and giving Britain more breathing room” amid the cost-of-living crisis, his team said.
Delivering growth and devolving power to regional communities are also expected to feature.
Also on Monday he is likely to announce his senior cabinet appointments, with all eyes on who will replace Rachel Reeves as finance minister.
The former mayor of Greater Manchester, nicknamed the “King of the North”, has been parachuted in by the Labour Party, after Starmer resigned last month, with MPs viewing him as the party’s best chance of reining in Nigel Farage’s anti-immigration Reform UK party.
‘Bigger, bolder’
Among Burnham’s most urgent challenges will be a tepid economy, high government borrowing costs, a ballooning welfare bill and irregular migrants arriving in small boats that have fuelled support for Reform.
Unpredictable energy prices due to the US-Iran war and a volatile American president in Donald Trump also threaten to buffet his premiership.
Burnham told The Times he would take a “different approach to public spending, and to running the economy – more focused on early investment, early intervention, setting people up for success, and much less paying for failure”.
He promised “early moves to help” with the cost of living, saying that while campaigning he heard the “pressure people feel around their finances”.
Starmer led Labour to power in July 2024 in a landslide election victory after 14 years of Conservative rule.
He announced that he would resign as prime minister and Labour Party leader in late June after a string of scandals, missteps and policy U-turns blighted his leadership.
Burnham, who only returned as an MP four weeks ago, has little room to manoeuvre amid sluggish economic growth, high public debt and strict financial rules requiring him to balance government spending against tax revenue.
‘Last chance’
Burnham was an MP between 2001 and 2017, serving as a minister in the governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.
He has since reinvented himself as a man of the people, melding a relaxed, folksy style with slick social media videos.
However, he has only three years to turn things around, with Reform leading in polls ahead of the next general election expected in 2029.
Burnham told supporters on Friday his Labour takeover was the “last chance” for the party to get things right.
Critics have accused Starmer’s government of being under-prepared for power when he was elected in July 2024.
Burnham has insisted he has a “plan”.
However, his swift “coronation” as Labour leader has raised questions on how he will achieve his aims.
His first policy announcement came on Saturday when he scrapped Starmer’s flagship nationwide digital ID scheme, estimated to cost £1.8 billion over three years.
A spokesman said the time and resources would be diverted “to where it’s most needed, such as helping with the cost of living”.

sources.news_title: Come Meet Britain's Next Worst Prime Minister Ever
sources.text:
Following King Charles III's formal request to form a new government on Monday, new U.K. Labour Leader Andy Burnham takes Keir Starmer's place as Britain's next worst prime minister ever. "I now pass the baton to Andy Burnham, I wish him every success. He has my full support," Starmer said to anyone still listening.
It won't be easy topping — bottoming? — Starmer's record of increasing Islamification, two-tier justice, and economic decline, but I have faith in Burnham's ability to do so. At the very least, there's certainly no doubting his willingness to try.
It seems like just last month [It was just last month, Steve —Editor] I wrote that "The U.K.'s most destructively feckless prime minister (since the last one)" would soon be history, but that Burnham "could prove Britain's final undoing."
I hate to be so pessimistic when it's only Monday, but take a look at this guy.
Burnham hasn't worked in the private sector in 30 years — as a writer, yuck! — serving in Parliament for two decades, both in and out of power. He held positions we don't even have here, like Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport, Shadow Secretary of State for Health, and Undersecretary for Taxing of Things We Haven't Yet Taxed.
Then he served as Mayor of Greater Manchester (2017-2026), until returning to Parliament earlier this year following a by-election (kind of like a special election year), seemingly for the sole purpose of taking a run at Starmer.
Mission: Accomplished.
As of this writing, Burnham is busy sacking various members of Starmer's cabinet, including Rachel Reeves as Chancellor, Steve Reed as Housing Secretary, Lord Hermer as Attorney General, Peter Kyle as Business Secretary, and the execrable David Lammy from his dual roles as Justice Secretary and Deputy PM.
But as one commenter on X warned: "Many people are loving all Burnham's sackings because of what they think about the politicians he's getting rid of. But don't cheer too enthusiastically because it's not at all clear that the new appointees will be any better."
The situation remains fluid, as they say, but Burnham has yet to name any replacements to serve in his cabinet. The name to keep an eye on — as I warned you last month — is the woman often called "the brains" behind Burnham's time as mayor, the Liberian-born daughter of lefty radicals: Miatta Fahnbulleh.
CutMyTaxUK reported last year that Fahnbulleh "was born in Liberia as part of a prominent leftist revolutionary family, has served as a junior energy & housing minister in the Starmer government before resigning to support Burnham." Previously, as the "former head of the far-left New Economics Foundation," she proved "adept at churning out socialist policy proposals."
Or as CMT-UK put it, "Keir Starmer has appointed a Housing Minister who hates private housing."
And guess what? Before even naming Fahnbulleh as Permanent Undersecretary for Ending Private Property, Politics UK reported that Burnham is considering introducing rent controls as part of his cost of living announcement on Tuesday. "We are looking at measures that could make a difference this year," Burnham said.
Tell me if this next item rings any bells, particularly for readers in California. "We ran a [homelessness] scheme every night. 600 beds," Burnham said Monday. "But we were the only place doing it. It taught me the only way is to do this together."
As mayor, he promised to end homelessness in Greater Manchester by 2020.
He didn't. But he sure spent a lot of money on it. Now he's taking his program nationwide, presumably.
What Britain needs is a national election that might correct Labour's lopsided majority in Parliament despite the party's massive unpopularity.
What they'll get is the country's next worst prime minister. Until the next one, I'm afraid.

sources.news_title: Burnham promises ‘different type of politics’ as new Prime Minister
sources.text:
Andy Burnham promises ‘different type of politics’ as he enters No 10 as new Prime Minister
'Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again'
Prime Minister Andy Burnham promised to win over voters “fed up with politics” and show the world that the UK can once again be a source of stability. Mr Burnham used his first speech as Prime Minister in Downing Street to promise to take power our of Westminster and give the public greater control over “life’s essentials”.
Speaking without the lectern used by his predecessors, Mr Burnham said he would set out help to address the cost-of-living squeeze. In his first promise as Prime Minister he said he would “end rough sleeping in our country”.
Mr Burnham, who was met with cheers by supporters in Downing Street, said: “I am acutely conscious that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street, the seventh prime minister since 2016, making this a moment for reflection and new resolution.
“It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge. Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again.”
He concluded his first speech as Prime Minister by urging people to “pull with me” to “build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity”.
Distant shouts of ‘No Rosebank’ could be heard from protesters outside the street amid reports Mr Burnham could back new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea. But they were not loud enough to disrupt the new Prime Minister. A man could also be heard singing Beethoven’s Ode to Joy as Mr Burnham spoke.
A protester holding an EU flag also appeared on Horse Guard Road but only shouted once. They clapped as he pledged an end to rough sleeping.
The crowd behind Mr Burnham nodded as he spoke, and greeted him with hugs after the speech concluded.
Andy Burnham's speech in Downing Street in full:
“I have just come from Buckingham Palace, where I have accepted His Majesty the King’s invitation to form a Government.
“In doing so, I am acutely conscious that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street, the seventh prime minister since 2016, making this a moment for reflection and new resolution.
“It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge.
“Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again, and that is our challenge – to make politics work, to make it work better.
“I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you and I want to be honest with you – we have not been good enough, and we need to be better. We will be. We will make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years – a new political model and a new economic model.
“In the 1980s, Britain took some wrong turns. Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, large parts of the country deindustrialised, and they still haven’t recovered.
“Many feel as though they’re still in decline and they don’t have the ability to turn things around. And that’s why we will change politics to make it more collaborative, more about problem solving than point scoring.
“And we will take power out of here, and carry it into every postcode in the land, so that they can do more, and in doing more, build a new economy, where we put life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again, reindustrialising Britain using public procurement to back British industry.
“Later this year, I will bring forward a new plan for Britain, a 10-year plan, laying out a path from where we are now to where I believe we all want Britain to be, wherever we’re coming from, whatever party we support.
“But I can do something to give people some breathing space now, some help with the cost of living, and I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them.
“We will help more young people into work by changing the education system and giving them more support, more mental health support, and we will build more council homes.
“That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules, and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.
“We will help people to live well, building a more preventative state, investing in people’s success rather than paying for failure, and that work starts now.
“I will soon go through that door behind me and issue my first instruction to end rough sleeping in our country.
“It’s about putting the right values and the right standards at the heart of government. I will put the care of people at the heart of everything I do.
“I will give this my all, and I ask you all to pull with me. Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose, and positivity.
“Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again, the moment we bring back hope.
“Thank you very much, everybody.”

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham takes charge as U.K.’s new Prime Minister
sources.text:
Former Manchester Mayor, Andrew Burnham, was appointed Prime Minister of the U.K. on Monday (July 20, 2026), its seventh in a decade. Mr. Burnham described the moment as a “circuit breaker”, as he promised to usher in a new political and social model for the country, taking power out of London and spreading it across the regions of the U.K.
The outgoing Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who had made history two years ago, when he led the Labour Party in one of the largest victories in modern times, made history again on Monday (July 20, 2026), but this time for becoming the U.K.’s shortest serving Labour Prime Minister
“I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything that we have achieved,” Mr. Starmer said in brief remarks outside on Downing Street, as he wished his successor “every success”.
Editorial | Downing streak: On the Starmer resignation, British politics
“We will make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years: a new political model and a new economic model,” Mr. Burnham said outside No.10 Downing Street, minutes after he was ceremonially invited to form a government by Britain’s Monarch King Charles III. Mr Burnham’s wife, the Dutch-born Marie-France van Heel, was also present as were large numbers of the Prime Minister’s supporters, including his mother and Josh Simons, the MP who vacated his Makerfield seat, so Mr Burnham could win it and return to Westminster.
“I am acutely conscious that I am … the seventh Prime Minister since 2016, making this a moment for reflection and new resolution,” Mr. Burnham said, adding that Britain needed to show the world it could regain its stability. He went on to add that the U.K. had taken wrong turns since the 1980s, by privatizing economic power and centralizing political power.
Andy Burnham: U.K.’s latest PM | Infographics
He reiterated his messages from recent months including his wish to see greater greater public control of utilities, supporting supporting young people to enter and stay in the workforce to bring down the welfare bill and spreading power more evenly across the U.K.
“…We will take power out of here and carry it into every postcode in the land,” he said. Mr Burnham had said in recent weeks that he would create a ‘No. 10 North’ — a hub office in Manchester to manage the redistribution of power. His first actions in office on Monday would be to “end rough sleeping [homelessness]” in the U.K., Mr. Burnham said.
The U.K. would have a new ten year plan, later this year, Mr. Burnham said, adding that he would issue more immediate orders starting Tuesday, to help with the cost of living along with details on how he would fund this. His first action in office on Monday would be to “end rough sleeping [homelessness]” in the U.K.
Mr Burnham did not mention Mr. Starmer’s name during his remarks, although he paid tribute to the man he ousted, on Friday, after accepting the leadership of their party. Mr. Burnham has had longstanding leadership ambitions; he tried unsuccessfully to become party Leader in 2010 and 2015.
The new Prime Minister has used the word ‘Manchesterism’ to describe his policies – which included the unification of Manchester’s public transport networks under greater public oversight. Little, however, is known about Mr. Burnham’s foreign policy generally and regarding the U.K.-India relationship.
The 56-year-old Mr, Burnham is pro-European; he has said previously that he hopes to see the U.K. back in the E.U. during his lifetime although he said he would not act to bring that about during his term in office. He apologized in recent days for Labour’s initial position on the Israel-Gaza conflict and has promised firmer actions against Israel. He appears to be pro-NATO and has indicated he will be bound by Mr. Starmer’s £15 billion defence investment plan which was announced in recent days. Mr. Burhnam recently said that British support for Ukraine “will not waiver” and that the U.S. was the county’s most important security ally. The new Prime Minister has committed to keeping Jonathan Powell in post as the U.K.’s national security adviser.
Keir Starmer resigns
Roughly an hour and a half before Mr Burnham’s speech, Mr Starmer had spoken outside No. 10, surrounded by his wife Victoria, supporters and members of his administration — including outgoing Chancellor of the Exchequer Rachel Reeves, Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy and London’s mayor Sadiq Khan.
Mr. Starmer, a centrist, struggled to hold Labour together since 2024, with internecine battles growing over policy differences ranging from welfare spending to Labour not taking a strong enough stance against Israel for its killing of civilians in Gaza.
Mr. Starmer’s credibility within the party took a further hit around his appointment of a controversial U.S. envoy and the resignation of several of his key staffers. His relationship with union leaders began to sour when he was still Leader of the Opposition, after he sacked an MP who had made an unauthorised media appearance alongside rail workers on a picket line. These ties frayed further despite his government passing the Employment Rights Acts 2025 to strengthen certain rights for workers. For instance, Labour lost support among energy workers over net-zero policies.
Reports of his managerial style within the party and the Cabinet also cost Mr. Starmer support from his colleagues. The final blows to Mr Starmer’s position came after Labour lost a crucial byelection to the Greens in the north west of England this year, followed by a major defeat to Reform in English council elections and losses to other parties in the Welsh and Scottish Assembly elections in May.
Mr. Starmer was given an emotional farewell during the weekly parliamentary Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs) last week, with colleagues and Opposition leaders praising him. In speeches, social media posts and interviews, Mr. Starmer and some of his colleagues — including Mr. Burnham — have sought in recent days to clearly articulate the outgoing Prime Minister’s achievements as a means to give Mr. Starmer’s exit dignity and order.
The message has included Mr. Starmer being responsible for Labour’s return from the political wilderness in 2024, actions to tackle child poverty in the U.K. such as the two-child benefit cap, strengthening workers’ and tenants’ rights, cutting wait times for medical appointments in the public healthcare system, and his support for Ukraine.
Watch | U.K. PM Keir Starmer resigns: What went wrong?
In his farewell address, Mr. Starmer said Britain’s reputation on the world stage had “been greatly enhanced”.
“We face a world now where our enemies will stop at nothing to divide us, because of our values, our freedom, our decency, and frankly, because of our unflinching resolve towards the brave people of Ukraine,” Mr. Starmer said, without naming Russia.
The outgoing Prime Minister had visited both Kyiv and Paris during his last week in office, receiving one of France’s highest national awards, the Légion d’Honneur, from French President Emmanuel Macron for his work in working with France to enhance European security. Mr. Starmer had launched a “reset” of the U.K.’s relations with the European Union following the country’s exit from the bloc under the Conservatives in 2016. Last week, a trade deal with India — talks for which began under the Conservatives — came into force. Mr. Starmer had vowed a “reset” of ties with India and the Indian government in 2023, in the face of tensions due to Labour’s earlier position on Kashmir and fraying support for Labour among Indian Britons.
As he returned to the backbenches, Mr. Starmer had fought to stay on in post — including by opposing Mr. Burnham’s attempts to contest a byelection in February. However, when a colleague vacated the Makerfield parliamentary seat so Mr. Burnham could contest it, Labour’s leadership team, including Mr. Starmer were compelled to permit it. Mr. Burnham won that election on June 18 and returned to Westminster.
At PMQs last week, Mr Starmer said he “wholeheartedly” supported his successor. Asked what advice he would give the incoming Prime Minister, Mr. Starmer had said that he would provide counsel “privately, when asked, not publicly, when not asked”.

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham Is Officially U.K. Prime Minister
sources.text:
Andy Burnham is, officially, the U.K.’s seventh Prime Minister in 10 years.
The 56-year-old has been named Britain’s new political leader and begins his stint in office from Monday, after being named leader of the Labour Party and meeting with the King, who invited Burnham to form a government. It is unclear if culture secretary Lisa Nandy, currently responsible for shaping industry policy around British film and TV and securing funding for the BFI, will remain in her post in Burnham’s cabinet. A reshuffle is imminent, but the two are long-time friends and allies in British politics.
Related Stories
Britons knew Burnham would be PM weeks before this announcement. His predecessor, Keir Starmer, was pushed into resigning by his own party following months of speculation that he was deeply unpopular among Labour ministers. Starmer’s critics said he tried too hard to pander to Conservative and Reform voters on issues such as Gaza, transgender rights, as well as immigration and measures to tackle soaring inequality.
Ultimately, Starmer simply wasn’t deemed a particularly strong leader for Britain. Enter Burnham, whose supporters believe he can bring the fight to Nigel Farage’s far-right Reform U.K. at the next general election, while maybe even winning over some Green Party voters while he’s at it.
Burnham was born in a suburb of Liverpool and joined the Labour Party at 15 years old. After studying at Cambridge University, he slowly rose through the U.K.’s political ranks and worked in government for former PMs Tony Blair and Gordon Brown. He’d later take on shadow secretary roles for Ed Miliband and Jeremy Corbyn, though through this time also launched multiple (and unsuccessful) campaigns to become Labour Party leader.
From 2017 until 2026, Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester, a position that earned him an image as a real “man of the people.” Over the last decade, his superpower has been acquiring an incredibly broad appeal across the north of England. Part of this is thanks to his instrumental role in introducing and passing the Hillsborough Law, legislation designed to prevent state cover-ups following public disasters and scandals. It earns its name from the Hillsborough disaster in 1989, which saw 97 Liverpool fans killed in a crowd crush at a soccer game, and the decades-long fight by victims’ families to pry the truth out of authorities.
He sits closer to Corbyn than Starmer or Blair on the left, and has even been branded “King of the North” for his anti-Westminster approach. This will be one of the central themes of Burnham’s government: pushing power out of London and into regional political hubs, as well as bolstering public transport to northern cities and tackling homelessness and social housing.
But Burnham will have to traverse some pretty bumpy political terrain here in Britain, with far-right politicians committed to weaponizing immigration policies and stoking the flames of division. Farage’s Reform, in particular, is eyeing a win in the next election — which will take place no later than August 2029 — though Kemi Badenoch’s Tory Party is increasingly taking a far-right stance on certain policies to claw back some of those voters lost to Reform.
Burnham has wanted to lead the Labour Party for much of his political career, and now faces an uphill battle in appointing a competent chancellor, finding £9 billion ($12 billion) for Britain’s defense, protecting the NHS, building the 1.5 million homes Labour promised in their manifesto, and getting over a million young people into work amid a brutal job market.
Add on top of this the fine line he has to walk on immigration, policing, and Gaza, and Burnham would be forgiven for feeling a little daunted. He maintains he is not. “I hear you. We have not been good enough and we need to be better. We will be,” he said from outside the Prime Minister’s official residence, 10 Downing Street, on Monday afternoon.
“We will make this moment a circuit-breaker for Britain and there will be a new political model,” he added. “I will put the care of people at the heart of everything I do. I will give this my all, and I ask you all to pull with me. Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose, and positivity. Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again — the moment we bring back hope.”
