sources.news_title: Burnham officially installed by the King after Starmer bows out
Andy Burnham is now the UK's fifth Prime Minister in four years
sources.text:
Andy Burnham is the UK’s new Prime Minister, taking over from Keir Starmer as the country’s seventh leader since the Brexit vote in 2016.
The former Mayor of Greater Manchester accepted an invitation to form a new government in a meeting with King Charles, shortly after Sir Keir formally told the monarch he is resigning.
Sir Keir quit with a speech outside Number 10 before formally offering his resignation to the King at Buckingham Palace.
Mr Burnham will soon begin appointing the top members of his Cabinet, with uncertainty still swirling around his picks for roles including Chancellor, Home Secretary and Foreign Secretary.
Follow Metro’s politics live blog here for all the latest updates.
Make sense of the mad world of British politics
Get analysis of the latest stories – including Andy Burnham's rise to Number 10 – direct to your inbox from Metro’s Senior Politics Reporter Craig Munro. Sign up here.
In his maiden speech to crowds outside Number 10, Mr Burnham said his first instruction will be to ‘end rough sleeping in our country’, and he will set out a ten-year plan to help with the cost of living and give people ‘breathing space’.
The moment marks the culmination of a spectacularly busy month for Mr Burnham, since he was confirmed as winner of the Makerfield by-election on June 19.
After spending the past nine years as Manchester’s mayor, he has been introducing himself to Labour MPs – many of whom he had never met before.
He became their leader at a special conference in London on Friday, after a contest where he faced no serious opposition.
The new PM has also been getting familiar with a Westminster Parliament that he has described as ‘more fragmented’ and ‘unhappier’ than the one he left in 2017.
Meanwhile, he has been dropping hints about his plans for power in a fewinterviews.
It is expected that his government will bring in new measures to help Brits struggling with the cost of living in the coming days
In an interview with the Sunday Times, Burnham said the country ‘will see early moves to help’, adding: ‘It’s all about helping people.’
Yesterday morning, he confirmed one of his first big decisions – scrapping the digital ID plans that were championed by Starmer’s government in what he called a ‘reset of priorities’.
He has also argued for a change in culture at Westminster, switching to a more collaborative and less combative approach between different parties and factions.
But the country’s latest leader faces a raft of serious challenges as he enters office, including weak economic growth and a war in Iran that is on the verge of spiralling out of control again.
He will have to face finding the funding for the Defence Investment Plan, tackling the NEET crisis highlighted by the Milburn Review, and reforming the social care system.
In the Makerfield by-election campaign and his media appearances since, Burnham has argued for devolution as the best means of pulling the UK out of its rut.
Speaking at the People’s History Museum in Manchester last month, he said he would set up an ‘extended operation’ of Downing Street in the city, dubbed ‘No 10 North’.
This office would be the ‘nerve centre for a rewired Britain’, he said, acting as the ‘conduit’ for redistributing power from Whitehall to Mayors and other regional leaders around the country.
However, in his speech outside No 10 today is he expected to say he is ‘acutely conscious’ that he is the UK’s fifth prime minister in the past four years.
He will say this underlines why the country requires more stability and responsibility in politics.
If he does not choose to go to the public early for a snap general election – which would give him an opportunity to run on his own manifesto, rather than Labour’s 2024 one – he will have three years before the next one is due.
With his party still languishing far below Reform UK in the polls, Burnham will need to pull off a remarkable feat of resurrection if he is to avoid the same fate as his short-term predecessors.

Former mayor of Manchester Burnham returned to Parliament in June after securing victory in the Makerfield by‑election, having previously served as mayor between 2017 and 2026. Last week, he was crowned as the new leader of the Labour Party in a largely uncontested race.
In his first speech as Labour leader, Mr Burnham said he wanted to give people “breathing room” amid rising living costs. The Prime Minister is expected to set out his Cabinet later on Monday, with appointments yet to be disclosed.
Earlier, departing Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer gave a farewell address outside Downing Street, saying that he 'changed' the Labour Party, making it 'fit to lead'.
"I'm about to visit His Majesty The King and offer my resignation to close the book on my time as Prime Minister," he began. "My work is done. In six and a half years, I took our party from a historic defeat in 2019 - changed it, so it was fit to face the country, and won a landslide general election victory in 2024.
"It has been the privilege of my life to serve you and this great country as Prime Minister. And I am confident that Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago."
Reports have suggested cost-of-living support offered by Burnham could include action on energy bills, including allowing more oil and gas drilling in the North Sea.
Environmental campaigners have urged him to stick to Labour’s 2024 manifesto, which promised not to issue new licences for North Sea drilling, arguing they would not reduce energy bills. Mr Burnham could also face a decision on whether to temporarily nationalise Thames Water as the firm struggles with a £20 billion debt pile.

sources.news_title: Britain’s new prime minister Andy Burnham ‘kissed hands’ with King Charles
sources.text:
On the eve of the tenth anniversary of Brexit, Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced that he would step down as Britain’s prime minister. Initially, people thought that Starmer wouldn’t end up leaving Downing Street until August or September, but Labour did something and now Starmer is officially gone as PM. He made his farewell address earlier today, with his staff and his wife behind him, and then he was gone. Well, no, not really – after his farewell address, Starmer had to go to Buckingham Palace to formally resign. Just minutes after Starmer left the palace, Andy Burnham turned up to kiss the king’s sausage fingers.
The man dubbed the “King of the North” became the new British prime minister Monday, the latest in a revolving door of leaders trying to halt a decade of political turbulence and economic stagnation in the United Kingdom. Burnham, 56, was appointed unchallenged after the unpopular Keir Starmer agreed to step down last month following a series of election defeats, U-turns and scandals.
Both Starmer and Burnham come from the same center-left Labour Party, and in the United Kingdom ruling parties can change leaders — and therefore the prime minister — in the middle of an election cycle without anyone voting. That said, Burnham has promised radical change after taking office following a morning of royal formality, though he already faces infighting over his Cabinet selections.
Making his first speech as prime minister outside No.10 Downing St., Burnham vowed a “circuit breaker for Britain” that would involve “the biggest changes of the past 40 years.” In keeping with the more casual style he’s sought to project, Burnham eschewed the lectern favored by his predecessors, instead speaking while standing freely in the famous street. “I know people are fed up with politics — I hear you,” he said, promising to “bring back hope” to the country.
The incoming leader has a heaving inbox: how to solve Britain’s cost-of-living crisis, revive its ailing National Health Service, and navigate bitter debates over immigration and Europe. He must also fend off the challenge from Reform UK, the hard-right party led by Donald Trump ally Nigel Farage, which tops the polls.
Monday started with the pageantry of a now familiar political handover (Burnham being Britain’s seventh prime minister in a little more than a decade and the fifth in four years).
He had already replaced Starmer as Labour leader. Then, early Monday, Starmer declared “my work is done” as he delivered a farewell speech outside his official residence at No. 10 Downing St. Starmer was then driven to Buckingham Palace, where he offered his resignation to King Charles III. After he left, Burnham arrived at the palace, and the king asked him to form a government. This ceremony is known as “kissing hands,” though new leaders aren’t actually expected to do that these days.
Once the new PM is inside the palace, the king’s team handles the imagery and which photos or videos are released. QEII and King Charles never released any photos or videos of a prime minister kneeling and kissing the sovereign’s hand, but I guarantee that the hand-kiss still happens. For all of Charles’ four prime ministers, he tends to release photos where he’s just greeting them with a handshake. Meanwhile you can look at plenty of places in the South that voted Brexit, these are usually very poor areas of high unemployment where people have lost hope (e.g. Clacton), making them easy prey for far right influencers on social media.

His early remarks are encouraging.
“We overtax people’s work and we under tax people’s wealth. I’m not sure the balance is right.” Finally a Labour prime minister who sounds like a Labour prime minister.
With a key advisor, an economist, who is anti royal funding and anti windsor.

I’d assume the British press will rip him to shreds. Is there any chance they won’t?

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham Becomes Seventh UK Prime Minister In 10 Years
sources.text:
We’ve been here before.
The UK has its seventh Prime Minister in a decade as Andy Burnham arrives at Buckingham Palace to greet King Charles III and be sworn in.
The former Greater Manchester Mayor has had an odd coronation, running unopposed to be leader of the Labour Party after his predecessor Keir Starmer stepped down amid dreadful poll ratings, a poor set of local election results and scandal involving former U.S. ambassador Peter Mandelson and Jeffrey Epstein. Starmer delivered his final speech before resigning this morning.
Burnham officially became Labour leader on Friday and Prime Minister today, which is ratified when he meets the King. Once he meets Charles III and is invited to form a government, he will give a speech outside his new 10 Downing Street home. The 56-year-old has been a well-known face in British politics for 20 years. He was Culture Secretary then Health Secretary in the Labour government of the late 2000s before twice unsuccesfully running to be Labour leader last decade.
Watch on Deadline
His near-decade run as Greater Manchester mayor led his popularity to soar owing to a set of popular policies, which he says he will attempt to roll out nationally, and he is widely seen as being far more charismatic than Starmer. He was a vocal backer of Greater Manchester’s successful bid to host the Edinburgh TV Festival, saying it would “open a new chapter defined by the unmistakable character that only Greater Manchester can bring.” Greater Manchester also houses the city of Salford, home to thousands of BBC employees after what is broadly viewed as one of the most successful out-of-London relocations the nation has ever seen.
Burnham’s in-tray is bulging as he moves into 10 Downing Street and he is set to pick his cabinet this afternoon, with the country facing a wealth of enormous challenges. Incredibly for a nation that is only supposed to have two per decade, he is the seventh Prime Minister in 10 years, the majority of whom have stood down rather than lost elections. His recent predecessors include Boris Johnson, Rishi Sunak and Liz Truss.
New Culture Sec
The film and TV industry will be keeping an extremely close eye on Burnham’s pick for Culture Sec. Lisa Nandy, current incumbent and a close Burnham ally, is reportedly leaving the role to run his new “super ministry” in the north of England.
Nandy is in the process of making some seriously big decisions, one being whether to intervene in Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery’s $110B merger, which won’t now be decided until early September.
Another is the future funding model of the BBC. Nandy recently signaled her backing for a plan to revamp the BBC license fee so that streaming sevice subscribers have to pay the £180 ($240) annual charge.
Other policy priorities include new legislation that would compel YouTube and TikTok to promote public service content from the BBC and other broadcasters.
The result of all these decisions could make Nandy’s successor rather unpopular in various circles across the pond.

sources.text:
Andy Burnham Is Now The British Prime Minister. He Is Vowing To Implement a New Economic Model
"We have not been good enough and we need to be better," Burnham said about the state of British politics.
Andy Burnham took office as the new British Prime Minister on Monday, vowing to implement a new economic model and end with years of instability.
"I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you, and I want to be honest with you, we have not been good enough and we need to be better," Burnham said outside of 10 Downing Street, the residence of the prime minister.
He went on to claim his leadership will be a "circuit-breaker" for Britain, which has seen seven prime minister in the past ten years since voting to leave the European Union.
Elsewhere in the speech, Burnham said he will unveil a plan for the next 10 years within months. He then vowed to announce immediate measures related to the cost of living on Tuesday and to explain how he will cost them.
He also said his first phone calls will be with U.S. President Donald Trump, as well as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Burnham previously served in several Cabinet positions under former Prime Minister Gordon Brown before becoming mayor of Greater Manchester in 2017, a role that raised his national profile during the COVID-19 pandemic and cemented his reputation as one of Labour's most influential regional leaders, gaining him the nickname "King in the North."
Burnham also pledged to fight against the rise of right-wing party Reform UK. However, the party's Nigel Farage is facing controversy of his own after facing allegations that he failed to declare a £5 million ($6.7 million) gift from cryptocurrency investor and Reform donor Christopher Harborne in 2024.

However, the move has backfired as his potential challengers refused to take part in the election, leaving him to only face a parody candidate: Count Binface, portrayed by comedian Jon Harvey, who has ran in several British parliamentary elections wearing a trash can on his head and a superhero-resembling suit and cape. sources.news_title: Andy Burnham Replaces Keir Starmer as UK’s Seventh Prime Minister in a Decade
sources.text:
Marrakech – Andy Burnham officially becomes Britain’s prime minister on Monday, replacing Keir Starmer after a political upheaval that made Starmer the shortest-serving Labour premier in history.
The 56-year-old former mayor of Greater Manchester – nicknamed the “King of the North” – takes office as the country’s 59th prime minister and the seventh to occupy 10 Downing Street since 2016. He enters the role pledging to “rewire” a nation struggling with stagnant wages, high taxes, and poorly performing public services.
The transition is expected to follow a carefully choreographed sequence. Starmer delivers a final statement outside Downing Street before traveling to Buckingham Palace to formally tender his resignation to King Charles III. The monarch then receives Burnham and asks him to form a government.
The ceremony, known as “kissing hands,” no longer involves any literal hand-kissing – the two simply shake hands during a brief private audience.
Once appointed, Burnham travels to Downing Street to deliver his first address as prime minister. He will declare himself “acutely aware” of how many leadership changes the country has endured, his office confirmed, and will call for “a more stable and responsible politics.”
A long road back to Westminster
Burnham’s path to Number 10 stretches back decades. He became a parliamentary researcher at 24, a special adviser at 28, and a member of parliament at 31. Over 16 years in the House of Commons, he served in both Tony Blair and Gordon Brown’s governments, rising to health secretary. He ran for the Labour leadership twice – in 2010 and 2015 – losing both times.
He left Westminster in 2017 to become Manchester’s mayor, during which he built a national profile through his advocacy for northern England during the COVID-19 pandemic and his campaigns for greater regional investment.
His return to parliament came only last month through a by-election in Makerfield, northwest England, triggered specifically to give him a path back to the leadership.
Burnham ran unopposed for Labour leader, securing nominations from 379 of the party’s 403 lawmakers.
Starmer’s departure followed a pattern now familiar in British politics. He announced on June 22 that he would step down after less than two years in office, declaring at his final Prime Minister’s Questions that “his political journey is over.” Less than two years after leading Labour to its largest parliamentary majority this century, his approval collapsed.
Policy missteps – cutting benefits for pensioners, accepting freebies, appointing Jeffrey Epstein-linked politician Peter Mandelson as ambassador to Washington – eroded public trust. Heavy losses in May’s local elections, with Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK surging, sealed his fate. He leaves office as the least popular prime minister on record.
Burnham inherits every one of those pressures. Average weekly pay, adjusted for inflation and excluding bonuses, has risen less than 1% since Labour took office in 2024, reaching £494 ($651). Taxes sit at multi-decade highs. Economic growth remains anemic.
In his first speech as Labour leader, Burnham described the moment as “the most significant change in our politics for 40 years,” promising a country where “life is more affordable, and all people and places are lifted from where they are now.” He pledged to govern for “the North, the South, the East and the West, for Scotland, Wales and for Northern Ireland.”
His early policy decisions are already drawing attention. Plans for a digital identity document were scrapped on Sunday. Thames Water, Britain’s largest water company, could be placed under temporary public control. His deputy, Lucy Powell, confirmed the government wants to “refocus and reprioritize” around cost-of-living concerns.
Burnham also makes history as the UK’s first Catholic prime minister – a distinction carrying weight in a country where centuries of legislation effectively barred Catholics from the office. He has credited “Catholic social teaching” as the foundation of his politics, with its emphasis on solidarity and local decision-making.
His most immediate task: appointing a cabinet. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has emerged as the frontrunner for chancellor, overtaking Energy Secretary Ed Miliband. Burnham offered no confirmation, urging his party to ignore “speculation.”
International reaction has been muted. US President Donald Trump remarked only that he suspects Burnham is “extremely liberal.” Russia expects no change in its strained relations with London. France’s foreign minister wished him well and hoped for “as much stability as possible.”

sources.news_title: From Greater Manchester mayor to No. 10: Andy Burnham set to become Britain's seventh PM in a decade
sources.text:
From Greater Manchester mayor to No. 10: Andy Burnham set to become Britain's seventh PM in a decade
Andy Burnham will then address the nation for the first time as prime minister in front of the famous black door of 10 Downing St.
Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester and new leader of the Labour Party, is taking the final steps on Monday to succeed Keir Starmer and become Britain's seventh prime minister in a decade.
The affable Burnham returned to Parliament in June by winning a risky special election and was sworn in as a member on July 12, hours after the unpopular Starmer announced his resignation to end a tenure of just two years in office.
Starmer will travel the mile from Downing Street to Buckingham Palace to formally tell King Charles III that he is resigning.
Also Read | UK’s economic, migration and Trump issues await Burnham at ‘No. 10 North’
Soon after, the 56-year-old Burnham will go to the palace, and Charles will ask him to form a government. That is when he will officially become prime minister, a moment known as “kissing hands.”
What will happen at Buckingham Palace
Andy Burnham has been UK leader in waiting for the past week. But he does not become prime minister until King Charles says so.
That will happen today at Buckingham Palace in an exchange that embodies the fact that in this parliamentary democracy, the right to govern is still derived from royal authority.
The ceremony harkens back to a time when the king exercised supreme power and chose his preeminent minister, the prime minister, to run his government.
That has changed, of course. Modern Britain is a constitutional monarchy where the king’s powers are strictly limited by law and tradition. But centuries after real power was transferred to the elected House of Commons, many things retain echoes of the past.
One of those is the moment when the king formally asks a politician selected by his or her party to form the next government.
Also Read | All about challenges that Andy Burnham will face as UK prime minister
How Britain got to this point
Britain got its most recent prime minister just two years ago, when Keir Starmer led the Labour Party to a landslide election victory.
Starmer’s honeymoon was short-lived. A series of missteps and policy U-turns saw public support drain away. After dire local election results in May, the Labour Party took the nuclear option and forced him to resign.
Britain’s parliamentary democracy allows governing parties to change leaders mid-term, with the winner becoming prime minister without the need for a general election.
The next national election does not have to be held until 2029, five years from the last election in 2024, though Burnham can call one sooner if he wants.
Get ready to meet the chief mouser
Before the day is over, Andy Burnham is likely to encounter Larry the cat, the most famous permanent resident of No. 10 Downing Street.
The gray and white tabby has lived at the prime minister’s residence since 2011, surviving six of Burnham’s predecessors.
A one-time stray adopted to help combat a rodent problem, Larry now regally patrols Downing Street, often appearing just as visiting dignitaries arrive.
He already has been seen Monday morning, the center of attention in front of the polished black door.
Larry is the most stable thing in British politics, said photographer Justin Ng, one of the cat’s most frequent chroniclers.
"(He’s) like the night watchman of Downing Street,’" Ng said. "He’s looking out, looking out for people. People are reassured (by) his presence that things will carry on."
These days Larry has his own profile on the government website and more than 900,000 followers on X. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte recently stopped to say hello, but all leaders hope to be seen by his side.
Now he just has to win over Burnham’s dog, Axel. No problem, right?

It’s moving day at Downing Street
It’s a day of action at Downing Street, the British prime minister’s official residence.
Departing leader Keir Starmer will give a short farewell speech before going to Buckingham Palace to tender his resignation to King Charles III. The king will then invite new Labour Party leader Andy Burnham to the palace and ask him to form a government.
Burnham will then address the nation for the first time as prime minister in front of the famous black door of 10 Downing St.
Labour is hoping Burnham’s arrival will signal an end to the rapid turnover of UK leaders. He will be the country’s seventh prime minister since 2016.

sources.news_title: UK's Andy Burnham becomes PM as Trump slams Britain as 'Poverty Stricken Disaster'
sources.text:
Andy Burnham became the U.K.'s seventh prime minister in a decade on Monday, with investors and market watchers already questioning his policy agenda.
King Charles III formally asked Burnham to form a government at Buckingham Palace earlier on Monday, which Burnham confirmed he has accepted.
"We will make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward a new political model and a new economic model," Burnham said in his first speech as premier on Monday.
"[We will] build a new economy where we put life's essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable again, reindustrializing Britain using public procurement to back British industry," he added.
New era for North Sea oil?
U.S. President Donald Trump has welcomed Burnham's plan to fast-track oil and gas exploration in already-licensed fields in the North Sea.
Writing on Truth Social over the weekend, Trump called North Sea oil "invaluable," adding it will take the U.K. from a "Poverty Stricken Disaster, to one of the Richest Countries anywhere in the World!"
The British economy has struggled for momentum in recent years. U.K. GDP is projected to grow by just 0.8% in 2026, following growth of 1.3% and 1% in 2025 and 2024, respectively. High energy costs have been highlighted as a key issue, piling pressure on policymakers to ramp up North Sea oil production even as Britain pushes ahead with its net-zero carbon goals.
Independent estimates collated by the U.K Parliament project that new drilling and favorable conditions could increase domestic production to a total of 7.5 billion barrels of oil equivalent.
Burnham replaces outgoing Starmer
Starmer announced last month that he would step down from his post, after a series of policy U-turns, scandals over staffing appointments and a dramatic loss in Britain's local elections sparked calls for his resignation from within his own ranks. Starmer officially resigned earlier on Monday.
Burnham had no opponents in the race to lead the governing Labour Party.
He returned to parliament just weeks ago, after winning a by-election in Makerfield, a constituency in the north of England. Only sitting members of parliament can run to lead the Labour Party.
Before his return to Westminster, Burnham – nicknamed Labour's "King in the North" – served as the Mayor of Greater Manchester, one of the U.K.'s largest metropolitan areas. Prior to his near-decade mayoral tenure, he was a Labour MP and held cabinet positions under prime ministers Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.
"I am ready," Burnham told supporters on Friday as he officially became the leader of the Labour Party.
The prospect of Burnham, considered more left-leaning than Starmer, replacing the incumbent prime minister sent jitters through bond markets earlier this year. Investors in U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, appeared to be largely supportive of Starmer and his finance minister, Rachel Reeves, remaining in their roles, due to their commitment to rein in public borrowing and spending.
In his speech on Friday, Burnham promised to fix the "big things" such as social care policy, and criticized changes that occurred in Britain over the past few decades after "political power was centralized and economic power was privatized."
Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, told CNBC's Squawk Box Europe on Monday that markets will be "relieved" that Burnham is set to select home secretary Shabana Mahmood as chancellor, rather than the more left-leaning Ed Miliband.
"But as soon as we shift away from people onto politics, the markets will put them under a microscope," he added.
"Two months ago, UK markets recoiled at the prospect of new Labour leader Andy Burnham becoming prime minister," James Smith, developed markets economist at ING, wrote in a note on Monday. "Today, his arrival in Downing Street has been met with little more than a shrug."
"Risk premium in the bond markets looks contained. Most investors I speak to don't expect him to rock the boat this year, even if there are concerns about the fiscal trajectory further ahead," he added.

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham to promise cost of living ‘breathing room’ as he enters Downing Street
sources.text:
Andy Burnham is set to become prime minister as he prepares to enter Downing Street.
He is widely expected to deliver a speech outside 10 Downing Street in which he will pledge to bring "breathing room" to struggling households and more stable and responsible politics.
Allies say Mr Burnham will stress the need for “tangible” political stability and improvements in people’s daily lives while urging the nation to face up to the difficulties ahead with “reflection and resolution.”
Ahead of Mr Burnham's appointment, outgoing Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer is expected to make his own remarks outside No 10 before travelling to Buckingham Palace to officially resign.
Mr Burnham will then be invited by the King to form a government.
Both speeches are likely to proceed undisturbed after police banned the use of amplified music outside Downing Street during the handover.
Following his address, Mr Burnham is expected to begin naming his first Cabinet.
While he has kept details of his selections under wraps, senior figures including Ed Miliband and Shabana Mahmood are believed to be in consideration for the role of Chancellor.
Mr Burnham’s rise to the country’s top job marks a rapid turnaround, coming just weeks after his return to Westminster via the Makerfield by-election.
Unlike typical leadership transitions, he takes office without a full contest and has yet to set out a detailed plan for his premiership.
Mr Burnham emphasised a commitment to devolving power from Westminster and pledged to establish a “No 10 North” base in Manchester.
He has also promised a wider reset of government priorities and has already signalled that he will scrap Sir Keir’s digital ID scheme to focus resources on addressing the cost of living crisis.
In an interview with The Times, Mr Burnham said he had already spoken with Treasury officials about his early plans and underlined the need to help people “feel better.”
He said: "The breathing space point is a really serious one."
He revealed that complaints about frozen tax thresholds made during the Makerfield campaign had “lodged in his mind.”
Reports suggest that his first week in office could see new policies rolled out in that direction, potentially including action on energy bills.
Environmental campaigners have urged him to stick to Labour’s 2024 manifesto, which promised not to issue new licences for North Sea drilling, arguing they would not reduce energy bills.
Mr Burnham could also face a decision on whether to temporarily nationalise Thames Water, which is currently burdened by £20 billion of debt.
He has previously expressed support for greater public control of essential services.
Thames Water’s main creditors have said they are willing to discuss the issue with ministers to avoid the company entering the special administration regime.
Social care reform is another likely priority for Mr Burnham.
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey has called on Mr Burnham to work with other parties to tackle the social care crisis, calling for protection against “catastrophic costs” and a universal safety net for family carers.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has written to the incoming prime minister urging him to back new oil and gas licences, rule out tax rises, and work together to cut the welfare bill.
Mrs Badenoch said: "You will enter office without having set out a clear plan on any of the issues facing our country.
"You have refused calls to come to Parliament for questions from MPs, and you have not submitted yourself to serious media scrutiny.
"This is not a promising start."
Despite the criticisms and calls for collaboration, Mr Burnham enters office facing a complex set of urgent challenges—economic, political, and social—all against a backdrop of public demand for change.

sources.news_title: UK: Andy Burnham takes office as seventh PM in 10 years
sources.text:
UK: Andy Burnham takes office as seventh PM in 10 years
July 20, 2026Newly-minted Labour Party leader Andy Burnham has met with the UK's King Charles III on Monday, the traditional final step in becoming the country's head of government.
Burnham is the seventh British prime minister in the last 10 years since the UK voted to leave the European Union.
His predecessor Keir Starmer announced that he was stepping aside in June after several Cabinet ministers resigned amid plummeting poll numbers and questions about his leadership.
Former mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham managed to win a risky special election in June in order to re-enter parliament.
Burnham promises to 'bring hope back' in first speech
Speaking for the first time outside his new home of 10 Downing Street, Burnham said that he was "acutely aware" of being the seventh prime minister in ten years, and promised to "make politics work better" than it has since the Brexit vote.
"I know people at home are fed up with politics, I hear you…we have not been good enough, and we need to be better," the PM said, before promising to bring about "the biggest changes in the last 40 years."
He then took aim at the privatization of public services and de-industrialization of Britain in the 1980s, without mentioning the names of any of his predecessors. Burnham said he would present a 10-year plan for a new economic and political model by the end of the year.
Adding that he was aware that the UK is facing a cost of living crisis right now, he promised to put forward a few proposals for easing the situation as early as tomorrow.
The Labour leader then said his very first concern was to "end rough sleeping in this country" and alleviate the housing crisis, before promising to "bring back hope" to all UK residents.
European leaders congratulate Burnham
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz offered his congratulations to Burnham in a social media message, adding that "Germany are the United Kingdom are close partners. I look forward to working together."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X that: "I look forward to working with you to strengthen the EU-UK partnership. For the security of our shared continent. And the prosperity of people on both sides of the Channel."
Also writing on X, France's Emmanuel Macron said that "in the face of the challenges that unite us, I hope that we will deepen our relationship in the service of our peoples and give new momentum to the partnership between the United Kingdom and the European Union."
Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelenskyy, whom Burnham has vowed to support, said he was "looking forward to our conversation later today," adding that the "foundation of our bilateral relations is stronger than ever, and we will continue to make each other stronger."
Starmer formally resigns
For Burnham to officially become prime minister, Keir Starmer had to first formally tender his resignation to King Charles III.
In prepared remarks as he left Downing Street, the outgoing leader highlighted his role in taking Labour from slumping poll numbers to a "landslide victory" two years ago.
"Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago," he said, claiming a better economy, shorter NHS wait times, and decreasing immigration.
He wished his successor "every success" and offered his full support.
Edited by: Rana Taha

sources.news_title: Socialist Takes Charge in UK, 7th New Prime Minister in Just a Decade
sources.text:
Socialist Takes Charge in UK, 7th New Prime Minister in Just a Decade
King Charles asked Labour Party leader Andy Burnham to form a new government today, making him Britain’s seventh prime minister in just a decade. 
     
Burnham, a self-identified socialist, pledged to bring a new political and economic model, criticizing the 1980s policies of Margaret Thatcher, who used free-market strategies to tame rampant inflation in the UK. 
Burnham served in Parliament for 16 years and as mayor of Greater Manchester, and has little experience of international affairs. He replaces former Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Starmer was forced to give up his position as leader of the Labour Party after losses in the 2026 local elections and controversial policy decisions.
Burnham now faces the immense task of kick-starting Britain's sluggish economy. He is also faced with the monumental problem of reducing government debt, which now equals more than 95% of gross domestic product, the highest since the early 1960s.
But his first task will be to fill the Cabinet, selecting leaders for the key positions of treasury chief, defense secretary, foreign secretary and home secretary, who controls immigration and policing.
The Reform UK party, which opposes unchecked immigration, had recently devastated Labour in local elections, which led to calls for Starmer’s resignation. But since the Labour Party still holds a majority in Parliament, its leader also becomes the U.K. prime minister.
Under Britain’s parliamentary democracy system, governing parties can change leaders midterm, with the winner becoming prime minister without the need for a general election.

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham becomes U.K. prime minister after Starmer resigns
sources.text:
Section Branding
Header Content
Andy Burnham becomes U.K. prime minister
Primary Content
LONDON — Keir Starmer is out, Andy Burnham is in.
On Monday, outgoing Prime Minister Starmer traveled to Buckingham Palace to tender his resignation to King Charles III. Shortly afterward, his successor, Andy Burnham, made the same journey and was invited by the king to form a new government.
Burnham then returned to Downing Street, where he delivered his first remarks as prime minister. He said, "it requires my generation of politicians to raise our game." He said politicians are "acknowledging that many voters have grown frustrated with politics."
"I want to be honest with you: we have not been good enough and we need to be better. We will be," Burnham said.
Burnham becomes the U.K.'s seventh prime minister in a decade, since Britons voted in June 2016 to leave the European Union. That decision ultimately shrank the British economy, triggered anger at the governing class, and contributed to a revolving door of prime ministers.
Starmer exits after two years
Starmer delivered his final speech outside 10 Downing Street earlier on Monday before heading to Buckingham Palace to formally resign as prime minister, declaring: "My work is done."
"In six and a half years I took our party from a historic defeat in 2019, changed it so it was fit to face the country, and won a landslide general election victory in 2024," Starmer said. He described serving as prime minister as "the privilege of my life" and said he was leaving office confident Britain was "stronger and fairer" than it was two years ago.
Closing his final address outside Downing Street, Starmer said, "I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything we have achieved."
Starmer led the U.K.'s center-left Labour Party to a landslide victory two years ago. But his personal approval ratings sank. Polls show voters believe he failed to deliver palpable change. He was also criticized for appointing Peter Mandelson, a close friend of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, as British ambassador to Washington. Starmer later fired Mandelson.
After Labour lost seats to a populist anti-immigration party in May's local elections, more of Starmer's own lawmakers joined calls for his removal.
Starmer resigned as Labour leader on June 22, and Burnham assumed that role Friday. Under Britain's parliamentary system, the ruling party can replace its leader — and therefore the prime minister — without a general election. The next election is not expected for another three years.
Burnham's first remarks as prime minister
Burnham previously served as a Member of Parliament for 16 years, holding several cabinet roles in the Labour governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown. He ran twice for the Labour leadership, receiving a nomination from Starmer during the 2015 contest, before leaving Parliament to become mayor of Greater Manchester.
As mayor, Burnham championed investment and devolution in the post-industrial region, and has pledged to bring a similar approach to the U.K. nationally. He returned to Parliament in a special election last month.
Standing outside Downing Street Burnham said he will announce measures to help with the cost of living on Tuesday, promising immediate support for households while setting out plans for longer-term change.
The new prime minister said his government would be "a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years."
"I can do something to give people some breathing space now, some help with the cost of living," Burnham said.
He added, "I will soon go through that door behind me and issue my first instruction: to end rough sleeping in our country." Burnham also said he would unveil a 10-year plan for Britain later this year.
A new prime minister, familiar challenges
Born and raised in the grittier north of England, Burnham has cultivated a working-class hero vibe, often wearing T-shirts rather than suits, and advocating for blue-collar workers. He moonlights as a DJ on Manchester's indie music scene. His social media videos have been compared to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's.
Polls show he's one of the most popular U.K. politicians.
In terms of policy, Burnham has said he'll scrap plans for digital ID cards, reverse the privatization of public transit and utilities, and devolve power away from the capital, London, toward municipal and regional authorities.
In recent days, there have been reports that Burnham might ease a ban on new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea — which won him immediate praise from President Trump on social media on Sunday. Trump wrote that with North Sea drilling, Burnham would transform the U.K. from "a Poverty Stricken Disaster, to one of the Richest Countries anywhere in the World!"
European leaders have begun congratulating Andy Burnham on becoming the U.K.'s new prime minister, with an invitation for his first foreign trip already arriving from Berlin.
Ireland's Prime Minister Micheál Martin welcomed Burnham's appointment, saying he hoped to work with him to strengthen ties between the U.K., Ireland and the European Union.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Britain and Germany remained "close allies and partners," and invited Burnham to visit Berlin.
But Burnham is likely to face some of the same challenges that stymied Starmer: Rising costs of living, slow growth, and that volatile American ally across the Atlantic.

sources.news_title: Can Andy Burnham Deliver the Change Britain Wants?
sources.text:
Britain enters a new political chapter on Monday as Andy Burnham becomes the country’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, replacing Keir Starmer and inheriting an economy weighed down by sluggish growth, rising living costs, and mounting pressure on public services.
After formally accepting the King’s invitation to form a government, Burnham will begin the difficult task of turning his campaign promise to “rewire Britain” into a governing agenda. His leadership marks one of the most significant shifts within the Labour Party in recent years, with supporters hoping he can restore public confidence and blunt the growing appeal of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
A New Direction for Labour
Burnham’s rise to the premiership follows weeks of political turmoil that culminated in Starmer’s departure after sustained criticism over Labour’s declining popularity.
Known as the “King of the North” for championing Greater Manchester during his time as mayor, Burnham built his national reputation by arguing that Britain’s economic and political system has become too heavily concentrated in London.
Stay ahead of the geopolitical week.
MD Briefing delivers expert analysis across five global fronts — the Indo-Pacific, energy, geoeconomics, European security, and the Middle East — every Monday morning. Free.
In his first address as prime minister, Burnham is expected to promise “a more stable and responsible politics,” arguing that Britain must confront its economic challenges honestly while rebuilding trust in government institutions.
Rather than presenting incremental reforms, Burnham has framed his premiership as an opportunity to fundamentally reshape how government operates and how economic growth is distributed across the country.
The Cabinet Will Signal His Priorities
One of Burnham’s earliest tests will be appointing a cabinet capable of delivering his ambitious domestic agenda.
Particular attention will focus on the appointment of Chancellor, one of the most influential positions in British government. Reports suggest Energy Secretary Ed Miliband and Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood are among the leading contenders, though Burnham has dismissed speculation and insisted no final decisions have been made.
Financial markets and Labour lawmakers alike will view the appointment as an early indication of whether Burnham intends to prioritize fiscal caution or more expansive public investment.
Cost of Living Takes Center Stage
Burnham has repeatedly argued that Britain’s political system has lost sight of the everyday concerns facing ordinary families.
His government is expected to prioritize tackling inflation, improving public services, boosting regional investment, and making housing and essential goods more affordable.
The emphasis reflects growing voter frustration over stagnant wages, rising household costs, and deteriorating public infrastructure—issues that have dominated British politics in recent years.
Burnham has also pledged to rebalance economic power away from London, giving local authorities greater control over transport, housing, and regional development.
Tough Decisions Await
The new government faces no shortage of immediate challenges.
Economic growth remains weak, productivity has stagnated, and pressure is mounting over taxation and public spending.
Britain’s struggling utility sector will also demand urgent attention. Thames Water, the country’s largest water company, remains burdened by heavy debt while facing criticism over repeated sewage discharges and infrastructure failures.
Senior Labour figures have already suggested stronger government intervention—including placing the company under special measures if necessary—highlighting Burnham’s willingness to expand public oversight of essential services.
Energy policy, oil and gas investment, and long-term industrial strategy are also expected to feature prominently during the first months of the new administration.
Political Pressure From Reform UK
Perhaps Burnham’s greatest political challenge will be containing the rapid rise of Reform UK, led by Nigel Farage.
Many Labour MPs viewed Burnham as the party’s strongest candidate to reconnect with working-class voters who have increasingly shifted toward populist alternatives.
His message of decentralization, economic fairness, and regional empowerment is designed to appeal directly to communities that feel neglected by successive governments.
Whether that strategy succeeds will largely determine Labour’s political fortunes ahead of the next general election.
What Comes Next?
The first 100 days of Burnham’s premiership will be closely watched.
Several key developments are expected:
- Cabinet appointments will reveal the government’s economic priorities and internal balance of power.
- An early economic package focused on easing cost-of-living pressures and stimulating growth is widely anticipated.
- Decisions on taxation and public spending will test Burnham’s promise to deliver change while maintaining fiscal responsibility.
- Reforms to public utilities could include greater government oversight of struggling infrastructure providers.
- Regional devolution plans are expected to advance Burnham’s long-standing campaign to shift more political and economic power away from Westminster.
Analysis
Andy Burnham enters Downing Street with one significant advantage over many recent British leaders: a clearly defined political identity. His reputation was built not in Westminster but through local government, where he consistently argued that Britain’s economic model has failed communities outside London.
However, governing nationally presents a far greater challenge than campaigning on reform. Burnham inherits limited fiscal room, weak economic growth, strained public finances, and a politically divided electorate. Delivering meaningful improvements in living standards while maintaining market confidence will require balancing ambitious reforms with economic discipline.
His promise to “rewire Britain” reflects broader public frustration with the country’s political and economic direction. Yet structural reforms—whether decentralizing power, rebuilding public services, or reforming utilities—take years to produce measurable results, while voters often expect immediate improvements.
Ultimately, Burnham’s success will not be judged by the rhetoric of renewal but by whether his government can deliver tangible economic gains, restore confidence in public institutions, and convince voters that Labour offers a more effective alternative to the growing populist challenge from Reform UK.
With information from Reuters.

sources.news_title: Live updates as new Prime Minister Andy Burnham enters Downing Street
sources.text:
Andy Burnham LIVE: Updates as Bridget Phillipson remains in cabinet under new PM
Andy Burnham gave his first speech as PM after officially taking over from Sir Keir Starmer today - here are all the latest updates
Andy Burnham has officially taken over the reins as Prime Minister, promising to give people “breathing room” against the rising cost of living. The new Labour leader entered 10 Downing Street today and delivered his first speech as PM on the steps.
Before the speech, Sir Keir Starmer made his own final address outside No 10 before heading to Buckingham Palace to formally resign before Mr Burnham met the King and was appointed Prime Minister. After his speech, Mr Burnham is expected to name his cabinet.
Monday caps a rapid transition for Mr Burnham, coming barely a month after he returned to Westminster following his victory in the Makerfield by-election. Without a full leadership contest, the new Prime Minister is yet to set out his full agenda for his premiership.
He has said he wants to devolve power away from Westminster as one of his key priorities, driving that agenda with a new “No 10 North” in Manchester, which he is expected to visit later in the week. Promising a “reset of priorities”, Mr Burnham has also announced he will scrap Sir Keir’s flagship digital ID programme to focus money and attention on the cost of living.
Big changes are already underway on Downing Street as Andy Burnham begins assembling his cabinet. Rachel Reeves is no longer Chancellor, with David Lammy and Peter Kyle also out of cabinet with more changes expected
His first week in office is expected to see policies aimed at making people’s lives easier. Follow our live updates below as events unfold today.
Key Events
Former Health Secretary Wes Streeting entered 10 Downing Street around 40 minutes ago.
Mr Streeting, who resigned from Sir Keir Starmer’s government, had been seen as a potential leadership candidate until he backed Andy Burnham.
Bridget Phillipson will remain a member of Cabinet as Minister for Women and Equalities in Andy Burnham’s Government, Downing Street has announced, but she is no longer education secretary.
Further appointments have been made to Andy Burnham's cabinet, and they are as follows:
- Angela Rayner has been appointed Housing Secretary.
- Jonathan Reynolds has been appointed Business Secretary.
- Lucy Powell is the new Education Secretary.
- Anneliese Midgley has been appointed as Chief Whip.
John Healey has said the new Government led by Andy Burnham "will meet our commitments on defence to our international allies".
The new Chancellor was asked by broadcasters on Monday night if he would meet a commitment to spend 3% of national economic output on defence by 2030.
Mr Healey expressed frustration that Sir Keir Starmer had not set out a clear timetable for the commitment when he resigned last month as defence secretary.
Asked if welfare cuts or new taxes were on the cards to meet the goal, Mr Healey said: "Fiscal control is the first duty of any chancellor. It is mine. And fiscal credibility is the bedrock for economic stability and for national security.
"You heard the Prime Minister this afternoon say, in this more dangerous world, we will meet our commitments on defence to our international allies."
Yvette Cooper said it was a "real honour to be appointed Health Secretary by Andy Burnham, 27 years after I worked on the first NHS cancer plan as a junior health minister".
In a statement shared on social media, the Health Secretary added: “I’m looking forward to working urgently to improve maternity services, to take forward plans for social care, and to once again play a part in supporting our National Health Service, Labour’s proudest achievement.
"Most of all I’m looking forward to working with the dedicated NHS staff, carers, healthcare professionals and volunteers on whom we all depend.
"In leaving the FCDO, let me pay tribute to the brilliant diplomats and ministers I worked with at the Foreign Office, and to my fellow foreign ministers from across the world, for all the work we did together to support Ukraine, to recognise the State of Palestine, to keep the spotlight on Sudan and to treat violence against women and girls as the global crisis it is.
"The partnerships we build abroad make us stronger at home."
Ed Miliband has shared this statement on social media: "It is a great honour and privilege to have been appointed by the Prime Minister to serve as Foreign Secretary.
"My parents came to Britain as Jewish refugees from the Nazis. To them, Britain was both a sanctuary and a beacon of hope in the global fight against fascism.
"I will carry my parents’ faith in that spirit of Britain to my role representing our country. I will be a Foreign Secretary who fights for Britain’s interests and our values of democracy, freedom and the rule of law on the world stage.
"The FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office) I lead will also be at the forefront of issues which pose profound and substantial threats to justice and equality in Britain and across the world.
"We will work with others on tackling the climate crisis, strengthening our partnerships for international development, and reforming our international institutions so they deliver for all countries, including the world’s poorest people."
Downing Street has announced that Yvette Cooper has been appointed Health Secretary, while Pat McFadden will remain as Work and Pensions Secretary.
Former foreign secretary Yvette Cooper and Pat McFadden have left Downing Street.
Mr McFadden, who has been Work and Pensions Secretary under Sir Keir Starmer, had been seen walking into No 10 with Ms Cooper shortly before 7pm on Monday.
Both Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson and Labour Deputy Leader Lucy Powell have entered Number 10, as Andy Burnham continues to make appointments to his cabinet.
Anneliese Midgley, the Labour MP for Knowsley who accompanied Andy Burnham to the despatch box when he was sworn in as an MP, has arrived at No 10.
Shabana Mahmood said the post of Home Secretary is “the best job in the business”, after Andy Burnham kept her in the role.
In a post on X, Ms Mahmood said she would continue with immigration reform.
She said: “It is an honour to remain as Home Secretary in Andy Burnham’s cabinet.
“I may be biased, but it’s the best job in the business.
“We have begun the work of major reform, to make our streets safer and our immigration system fair for all. Now let’s finish the job.”
New Chancellor John Healey says it is the “greatest privilege” to take on the role.
In a statement posted on X, he said: “It is the greatest privilege to be appointed Chancellor of the Exchequer by the Prime Minister.
“Together, we will build a new economy, build new hope and advance the working people of this country.
“Time to get on with the job.”
Former deputy prime minister Angela Rayner has entered No 10 as Andy Burnham’s Cabinet appointments continue.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has entered No 10 as Prime Minister Andy Burnham continues to make appointments to his Cabinet.
Pat McFadden has walked into No 10 as Andy Burnham is appointing his Cabinet.
Mr McFadden has been Work and Pensions Secretary under Sir Keir Starmer.
Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper has also entered No 10 – shortly before Ed Miliband was appointed to that role.
Louise Haigh has been named as Andy Burnham’s First Secretary of State, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and minister for the Cabinet Office.
She was previously the Secretary of State for Transport, from July to November 2024.
Shabana Mahmood will remain in the role of Home Secretary in Andy Burnham’s Cabinet.
She has worked in that position since September 5, 2025, under previous leader Sir Keir Starmer.
Former Labour leader Ed Miliband has been appointed as the Foreign Secretary under Andy Burnham.
It was thought he was being earmarked for a major role by the new Prime Minister, and this has proven to be the case.
John Healey has been named Chancellor in Andy Burnham’s first Government appointment, as he purged the Cabinet of loyalists of his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.
Mr Healey’s posting to the top of the Treasury came as a surprise to Westminster.
Mr Healey, who recently resigned as Sir Keir’s defence secretary in a row over military funding, replaces Rachel Reeves in the role and is seen as a safe pair of hands.
Nick Thomas-Symonds has said he will leave his post as the EU relations minister and paymaster general.
In a letter to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, he said: "I will support the new team of ministers from the backbenches and continue to serve the people of my home constituency of Torfaen, who, as always, remain my top priority."
Northern Ireland secretary Hilary Benn has announced he is leaving the role.
In a statement on the social media platform X, Mr Benn said: “It has been a great privilege to serve as Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and to work with the many wonderful people I have met over the last 2 years.
“I wish my successor all the very best in working with the Executive to protect stability, continuing to generate growth and investment and in taking forward the Troubles Bill which is so important for so many families.
“The Prime Minister will have my full support from the backbenches.”
Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed Andy Burnham’s assurance that the UK’s support for Ukraine would remain strong.
After speaking with the Prime Minister, the Ukrainian president wrote on X: “I was happy to speak with Andy Burnham and congratulate him on taking office as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.
“I truly appreciate that the support for Ukraine and our people will remain steadfast. Thank you for your warm words of respect for the Ukrainian people and for your condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed in Russia’s recent attacks.
“Ukraine and the United Kingdom have built the strongest partnership in the history of relations between our two countries, and we will certainly continue working to expand it even further.
“We agreed to discuss our future cooperation, including our work within the Anti-Ballistic Coalition, during a meeting in the near future. Thank you, Andy. Thank you, Britain!”
The Downing Street spokesperson continued: "Setting out his vision as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, the Prime Minister said he would be focused on ensuring reindustrialisation up and down the country to ensure good growth in every postcode.
"The Prime Minister also underlined his commitment to defence and security and said ensuring the security of the UK and its allies was at the top of his agenda.
"The president then updated on the situation in the Middle East, and the Prime Minister outlined the UK’s commitment to securing the movement of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to support global supply chains and drive down costs for businesses and families across the country."
Foreign Office minister Baroness Jenny Chapman of Darlington said she is leaving the Government, as she said cutting the aid budget had been “challenging” and required “much soul searching”.
Lady Chapman, who held a brief that covered international development and Latin America, said she would “always” be proud to have served in Sir Keir Starmer’s government.
She said: “It’s been a great honour to serve as international development minister, and in Keir Starmer’s cabinet. I’m disappointed to be leaving but wish the Prime Minister and his new team every success.
“Cutting the aid budget has been challenging and has required much soul searching, but I passionately believe thanks to the work we’ve done, we’re spending the money better than ever before.
"We have a modern strategy and approach, working in partnership with developing countries rather than in a paternalistic way, and keeping strong commitments on global health and humanitarian aid.”
She added: “The UK is once again a force for good internationally.”
Andy Burnham congratulated Donald Trump on the Fifa World Cup during their first phone call, and said he hoped he could show the US president around Manchester during a future visit.
A Downing Street spokesperson said: "The Prime Minister spoke to the President of the United States, Donald Trump, shortly after taking office this afternoon.
"The Prime Minister began by congratulating the president on a successful World Cup and agreed that England had an excellent tournament.
"The Prime Minister also hoped that he would be able to show the president what Manchester had to offer during a visit in the future."
Ed Miliband and Shabana Mahmood, who had both been the subject of speculation they could become chancellor, walked into No 10 together.
Former defence secretary John Healey was the first person to enter No 10, indicating he could be in line for a senior role.
Darren Jones, who served as chief secretary to former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer, has said Andy Burnham told him that he “won’t be a part of his new cabinet”.
Mr Jones was chief secretary to the prime minister and chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, having previously been chief secretary to the Treasury.
Former defence secretary John Healey, who resigned from Sir Keir Starmer’s cabinet in a row over money for the armed forces, has walked into Number 10.
Jo Stevens is the latest departure from Andy Burnham's government. The MP has acted as the Secretary of State for Wales since 2024.
- Steve Reed - Housing Secretary
- Peter Kyle - Business Secretary
- Liz Kendall - Science and Technology Secretary
- Rachel Reeves - Chancellor of the Exchequer
- David Lammy - Deputy PM and Justice Secretary

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham becomes U.K.'s 7th prime minister in a decade
sources.text:
LONDON — Prime Minister Andy Burnham said politicians "need to be better" as he delivered his first speech Monday as Britain's new leader.
Burnham spoke for several minutes outside 10 Downing St., where he promised to end street sleeping by homeless people and deliver a "circuit breaker" for a system he says has taken wrong turns since the 1980s.
After weeks as leader-in-waiting, Burnham officially became prime minister during a meeting with King Charles III at Buckingham Palace, where the monarch asked him to form a government.
He succeeded Keir Starmer, on a day when Britain's political turbulence gave way, at least temporarily, to smooth choreography.
Buckingham Palace has released a photo of the king and Burnham shaking hands. The ceremony known as "kissing hands" marks the transfer of power.
The palace said in a statement that the king "received in audience the Rt. Hon. Andrew Burnham MP and requested him to form a new Administration. The Rt. Hon Andrew Burnham MP accepted The King's offer and kissed hands upon his appointment as Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury."
Burnham is the seventh U.K. prime minister since 2016 in a now well-rehearsed handover after replacing Starmer as leader of the center-left governing Labour Party on Friday.
Burnham said he was "acutely conscious" that of the revolving door he was walking through.
"This a moment for reflection and new resolution," he said. "It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge. Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again, and that is our challenge to make politics work, to make it work better."
Just over an hour earlier, Starmer made a short farewell speech outside the prime minister's residence, saying "my work is done."
The outgoing leader, forced to resign by his own party, said Britain is now "stronger and fairer than it was two years ago," when he took office.
"I go with good grace, I go with a smile and I go proud of everything that we have achieved," Starmer said before heading to Buckingham Palace to offer his resignation to the king. It was an offer "His Majesty was graciously pleased to accept," the palace said in a statement.
Burnham then went to the palace in his turn and Charles will ask him to form a government. That's when he officially becomes prime minister, a moment known as "kissing hands."
The king's role harkens back to a time when the monarch exercised supreme power and chose a prime minister to run the government. Today, the king has no political power, but the monarch still officially offers the job to the leader of the party that can command a majority in the House of Commons. No hand-kissing is involved.
Britain's parliamentary democracy allows governing parties to change leaders, and thus prime ministers, without the need for a general election. The next national poll doesn't have to be held until 2029, though Burnham can call one sooner if he wants.
From the palace, Burnham will go to Downing Street, where he will make his first speech as prime minister.
A spokesperson said Burnham will say that he's "acutely aware" of how many changes of leader the country has been through in the past decade, and will pledge to restore stability.
Starmer said much the same when he took office two years ago. Last month he announced he would resign after missteps and judgment errors that eroded his standing with his party and the public.
Burnham was the only candidate in a contest to become the party's new leader, securing nominations from 379 of the 403 Labour lawmakers in the House of Commons.
The former mayor of Greater Manchester has pledged to make politics "less toxic," improve living standards across the country and "bring back the hope we have all been missing."
"I will work to build a new politics," he said after becoming Labour leader on Friday. "The country is crying out for it."
Critics and supporters alike will soon be clamoring for details of how Burnham plans to fulfill his pledges.
"Fundamentally, it only will work if you can generate significant economic growth, because it's the lack of growth that's really holding the country back," said Joshi Herrmann, who has followed Burnham's career as founder of Manchester news site The Mill.
Attention will quickly turn to who Burnham will appoint to his Cabinet. He's expected to make changes to Starmer's top team, especially to the biggest jobs of Treasury chief, foreign secretary and home secretary.
In his first speech as Labour leader, Burnham praised Starmer's achievements, saying he would "build on the foundation laid" by his predecessor.
Starmer became Labour leader in 2020 after one of the party's worst election defeats, and led it to a landslide victory four years later. But he was soon defeated by the challenges of governing.
At his final Prime Minister's Questions session in Parliament on Wednesday, Starmer defended his government's record on the international stage — especially its support for Ukraine — and its domestic policy achievements. He mentioned stronger protections for working people, a reduction in child poverty, a law designed to stop official cover-ups after tragedies, and higher defense spending.
"In six and a half years, I took our party from a historic defeat in 2019, changed it so it was fit to face the country and won a landslide general election victory in 2024," Starmer said in his final remarks before leaving Downing St, hand-in-hand with his wife Victoria.
"Since then, it has been the privilege of my life to serve you and this great country as prime minister. I am confident that Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago."
